edges.relationship: As Dagbovie recounts, Du Bois valued Woodson’s factual research but criticized his church history for failing to interpret the inner meanings of Black religious experience.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Dagbovie’s 2012 study, printed17–18 and note29, reconstructs Du Bois’s 1922 review. The acknowledgment of useful fact-finding and the earlier praise for Woodson’s education study remain alongside the methodological objection. Du Bois’s original Freeman review,4October1922,92–93, and Aptheker’s 1977 reprint,67–68, were not independently read. Woodson’s full church history remains unread; this is an attributed judgment, not an editorial finding of inadequacy.

edges.relationship: Du Bois recommends the first edition of Woodson’s The Negro in Our History as a resource for Black historical education.
edges.evidence_note: Own1935 essay, printed333, expressly recommends the first edition alongside Brawley and the jointly credited Cromwell, Turner and Dykes reader, and also recommends Negro History Week. This records a particular endorsed teaching resource, not a formative influence or approval of all editions. Du Bois distinguishes education from a universal prescription for separate or mixed schools at335. The full Woodson textbook and its edition history were not read.

edges.relationship: Higginbotham recalls that her father’s devotion to Woodson’s historical mission led her into history, a commitment she later deepened through reading Woodson.
edges.evidence_note: Own oral-history testimony,16June2011, transcribed by Ashley Robertson in the2012 NPS study, printed185 and188. Albert N. D. Brooks is the essential intermediary; this does not make Woodson her personal academic supervisor. Higginbotham also identifies insufficient attention to African American women in the earlier scholars’ groundwork at188; admiration does not erase that qualification. Her father’s recollections, her childhood visits and her later reading remain distinct. Only selected transcript passages were read; no interview recording or full monograph reading is claimed.

edges.relationship: Charle recalls adapting Bourdieu’s analysis of the literary field to Zola, and pursuing the dialogue between history and sociology with his encouragement.
edges.evidence_note: Own2015 retrospective,75–76, places the1971–72 ENS seminar beside prior reading of jointly authored Bourdieu/Passeron books; Passeron’s credit remains. Own2007 email answer published2008,162, confirms intellectual fidelity while requiring historical correction of concepts taken from other times and objects. This supports an acknowledged, specific resource rather than doctrinal obedience or formal dissertation supervision. Later critical disagreement remains separately represented. Original seminar and cited monographs unread.

edges.relationship: Charle challenges the isolation of Manet in Bourdieu’s account of symbolic revolution, emphasizing collective artistic dissent, dealers and differentiated market dependence.
edges.evidence_note: Own2025 article,paragraphs17–24, with qualifications28–31: Charle credits the project’s achievements and Bourdieu’s more nuanced warnings against romantic rupture accounts. The2013 posthumous volume combines lectures with an unfinished manuscript coauthored with Marie-Claire Bourdieu; Charle’s own participation in its collective editing does not erase that credit or the work’s unfinished state. Public ResearchGate reproduction of the author’s article was read; publisher OpenEdition routes presented an Anubis check and were not bypassed. Full2013 book and later impressionism conference contribution unread.

edges.relationship: Charle and Roche jointly argue that Bourdieu’s historical sociology helps overcome academic divisions and requires historically situated concepts.

This is a specified shared argument, without inferred causal priority or identical positions elsewhere. Adjacent pieces by Honneth and Ernaux are separate authors’ work and are not assigned to Charle/Roche.

edges.relationship: Charle identifies methodological proximity to Noiriel’s sociohistory despite their different labels.
edges.evidence_note: Own December2007 email answer,published2008,162, rejects an unproductive terminology dispute while appreciating Noiriel’s and Michel Offerlé’s work and the work in their collection. Offerlé and the collective publication programme retain credit; no shared organization, identical interpretation or personal influence is inferred from this limited comparison. The books and collection were not freshly read.

edges.relationship: As Bantigny explains, Charle adopts Hartog’s regimes of historicity to study the socially uneven advance of modernity across the long nineteenth century.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Bantigny’s2013 review,opening paragraph ending with note3, identifies the conceptual resource and its historical application. Her account distinguishes adoption from debate about the concept. Hartog’s2003 book and2012 reedition are distinguished in her note3; Charle’s2011 monograph and Hartog’s underlying works remain unread here. Her mentions of Lévi-Strauss,Lefort and Koselleck describe Hartog’s antecedents, not proof of three direct transmissions to Charle.

edges.relationship: Charle credits the merits of the Lieux de mémoire project but argues that its popularity returned historians to cultural and national frames.
edges.evidence_note: Own December2007 answer,published2008,163–164, explicitly says that he participated without following the master-builder’s intended direction. The institutional bibliography identifies Pierre Nora as editor of the specific1986 and1992 Lieux volumes to which Charle contributed; the interview’s unnamed editor is identified through that metadata, not presented as an explicit spoken naming. This is a qualified objection to a project’s framing and reception, not a rejection of memory research or adjudication of every chapter. Original volumes unread.

edges.relationship: Calloway uses Crosby’s Columbian Exchange to frame colonization as an exchange of organisms and diseases that changed Native capacities for resistance.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2011 interview, displayed version updated2022; specific conceptual resource, not a sole-cause explanation or a dated origin of Calloway’s research. Crosby’s 1972 book remains unread. Calloway’s priority claim about epidemic scholarship is his assessment, not an independently established first.

edges.relationship: Calloway identifies Deloria’s critique of outside experts as a continuing caution for his own practice and accountability to Native communities.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview section3 explicitly includes himself among non-Native researchers made to reconsider their methods. The1969 collection remains unread; this is acknowledged methodological use, not an inference about Indigenous identity.

edges.relationship: Calloway draws on White’s account of negotiated Native power and cultural accommodation to unsettle an English-centered, east-to-west account of early America.
edges.evidence_note: Own2011 interview explains the particular resource; Parmenter1999 p124 separately identifies White alongside James Axtell and James Merrell in New Worlds for All. Their credit remains plural. Bailyn1995 also names White’s resource in Calloway’s Revolution book. These are distinct witnesses, consolidated in one contribution claim. The complete books and Calloway’s1992 review remain unread.

edges.relationship: Richter praises Bailyn’s colonial synthesis but challenges language and interpretation that minimize Native settlement, strategic choice and power in shaping colonial migration.
edges.evidence_note: Own Harvard Magazine review online14December2012/printJanuary–February2013. The objection concerns The Barbarous Years and its peopling framework, not every Bailyn work. Richter explicitly credits James Merrell’s language critique and uses Francis Jennings and Cynthia Van Zandt for the Susquehannock example; retain their credit without inventing endpoints. Praise and disagreement coexist. Bailyn’s full book and any reply remain unread; the apparent PDF link redirects to an accessibility notice, so no print-page collation is claimed.

edges.relationship: Wood uses Richter’s study of Iroquois captive warfare to question Taylor’s account of Native punishment and cross-cultural differences.
edges.evidence_note: Wood’s own2006 review expressly names Richter’s earlier study in the section2 discussion of captives. This records Wood’s specific scholarly use, not Richter’s endorsement of Wood’s criticism of Taylor. Richter’s1983 War and Culture is a bibliographic lead; Wood does not identify the title, and the match is unconfirmed. The article body and Taylor’s complete book remain unread; the detailed description is Wood’s account. Section1’s separate Facing East discussion and the later unnamed-anthropologists claim are not conflated.

edges.relationship: Roche credits Foucault’s histories of the clinic and madness with showing links between intellectual changes and practice and unsettling inherited categories.
edges.evidence_note: Own2016 answer, published2018, pp.160–161. His particular use coexists with his reservation about successive epistemes; it is not adoption of all Foucault’s philosophy. The original books and recording remain unread here.

edges.relationship: Roche questions whether successive epistemes can adequately connect intellectual change with social and cultural history, while valuing Foucault’s historical work.
edges.evidence_note: Same own answer distinguishes this reservation from his positive use of the clinic/madness studies and recognizes Foucault’s own awareness of the problem. Particular criticism, not wholesale rejection or independently checked interpretation of every book.

edges.relationship: Roche recalls the fascination of Braudel’s material-civilization history and The Mediterranean as resources encountered through reading.
edges.evidence_note: Own answers160–161 distinguish the1967 material-civilization volume from its1979 reworking. Roche explicitly denies being Braudel’s seminar student; a later presentation of his thesis is different from initial training. Complete Braudel books not read here.

edges.relationship: Roche credits Braudel’s global reach but argues that his formation limited access to the historical perspectives of indigenous populations.
edges.evidence_note: Own first-part answer, printed175, applies the qualification to Braudel and some contemporaries and recognizes exceptions. It is a particular perspective/access criticism, not denial that Braudel wrote world history or a blanket rejection of his work.

edges.relationship: Roche credits Labrousse’s contextual political history and advice to avoid another regional or urban monograph in shaping his research choices.
edges.evidence_note: Own recollection161–163 explicitly identifies him as a pupil and describes the advice. Alphonse Dupront separately accepted supervision of Roche’s self-devised academy thesis. No sole-supervisor claim; political contexts are not reduced to a food-crisis cause.

edges.relationship: Roche identifies Distinction as a repeated resource and credits Bourdieu and Passeron’s account of educational reproduction while qualifying his own use as less mechanical.
edges.evidence_note: Own answer162 preserves Passeron’s coauthorship and separately names Baudelot and Establet. Political contact and institutional support do not by themselves establish influence. This is specific acknowledged use; complete cited books unread.

edges.relationship: Levi uses Roche’s Ménétra as an example of contextual biography, then warns that this approach can make context too fixed for individuals to change it.
edges.evidence_note: Levi’s own1331 discussion, in Olivier Christin’s French translation, also recognizes rich results and a balance between individual lives and social systems. The subsequent warning concerns an approach exemplified by Roche, Davis and Venturi; it is not a categorical charge against all Roche’s work. Original Ménétra text unread.

edges.relationship: Roche praises The Foul and the Fragrant but questions whether its treatment of smells gives enough attention to social differentiation and changing relations between groups.
edges.evidence_note: Own first-part answer3, printed172, explicitly calls Le Miasme et la Jonquille a very good book before the reservation. This is a narrow methodological disagreement, not rejection of sensory history; the original book remains unread here.

edges.relationship: Roche identifies The Birth of a Consumer Society by McKendrick, Brewer and Plumb as a stimulus for his later consumption research.
edges.evidence_note: Own answer27, printed182, credits all three authors and distinguishes his1981 Le Peuple de Paris from the1982 book. The later stimulus is not projected backward into that earlier work. Archival parallels do not prove direct collaboration; he separately recalls only one meeting with Brewer. Original volume unread.

edges.relationship: Roche recalls contributing his study of booksellers’ classifications to Furet’s book-history inquiry and receiving Furet’s acknowledgment for it.
edges.evidence_note: Own retrospective answer15, printed164, specifically identifies Livre et Société and note16 in Furet’s text. The original Furet acknowledgment was not independently read here. This is a recalled research contribution, not an inference from knowing Furet or sole authorship of the inquiry.

edges.relationship: Roche and Vovelle’s jointly organized colloquia provide a teaching comparison of their exchanges over social history and methods.
edges.evidence_note: Roche’s own answer14 names both organizers and distinguishes1965/1967 meetings from1967/1973 publications. Undirected editorial comparison, not causal priority or identical methods. The complete proceedings and every participant’s argument remain unread.

edges.relationship: Roche recalls admiring Le Goff’s course on merchants and his published work while distinguishing that resource from membership in Le Goff’s student circle.
edges.evidence_note: Own answer20, printed167–168, explicitly says he attended the École normale course but did not enter the EHESS student circle. The later career conversation is a different episode; neither sole supervision nor a complete-book reading is asserted.

edges.relationship: Rodgers builds on Wiebe’s account of organizational change while treating bureaucratic social efficiency as one progressive language among several.
edges.evidence_note: Own1982 historiographical essay,117–118 and127/n59, praises the link between organizational transformation and one strand of thought while explicitly noting that Wiebe had already made qualifications that later inquiries swamped. This specified resource coexists with Rodgers’s criticism of simplification; it does not make Wiebe responsible for Rodgers’s entire three-language interpretation. The Search for Order and later1973 essay remain unread here.

edges.relationship: Rodgers argues that Wiebe’s organizational synthesis simplified progressive ideas and left the relation between professionalization and social visions insufficiently explained.
edges.evidence_note: Own1982 essay,118–119, qualifies the new-middle-class carrier thesis and distinguishes job control from a shared bureaucratic political ethos. He praises Wiebe’s account of organizational change and later credits his earlier qualifications,n59; this is not a wholesale rejection. Hays’s more sweeping functionalist explanation is a separate target and is not silently assigned to Wiebe.

edges.relationship: Rodgers disputes Hofstadter’s relatively prosperous framing of the Progressive Era, foregrounding acute labor crisis and conflict over corporate power.
edges.evidence_note: Own1982 essay120 and note33 explicitly contrasts Hofstadter’s framing with recent labor history. David Montgomery,Bruno Ramirez and Richard Edwards retain the supporting works’ separate credit. Rodgers also treats Hofstadter’s generation as having brilliantly launched a historiographical question at114; disagreement does not erase that assessment. The original Age of Reform and all cited labor books remain unread.

edges.relationship: Rodgers uses Lears’s account of fin-de-siècle ennui as one possible explanation for the middle-class appetite for muckraking.
edges.evidence_note: Own1982 essay124 explicitly identifies this thread with Lears and note47 specifies No Place of Grace(1981). It remains one tentative thread alongside political economy,utility monopolies and McCormick’s corruption-exposure account; no sole explanation or full agreement is claimed. Lears’s whole book remains unread.

edges.relationship: Rodgers draws on Higham’s account of Protestant social-gospel thinking as one resource for explaining progressive languages of social bonds.
edges.evidence_note: Own1982 essay126 and note55 explicitly use this resource alongside Robert M.Crunden,Joseph F.Kett and Clyde Griffen,whose separate credit remains essential. Rodgers leaves the transatlantic reconstruction and channels of transmission open;this does not attribute the whole three-language synthesis to Higham. Higham’s original1974 article was not freshly read.

edges.relationship: As Soll reconstructs, Rodgers challenges the reach of Pocock’s early republican-language paradigm and calls for political, social and cultural contexts beyond it.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Soll2010,printed22 and notes4–6,reconstructs Rodgers1992,37–38,and retains Rodgers’s acknowledgment of the republican debate’s contribution to constitutional history. The claim is limited to the strong early paradigm,not all of Pocock’s changing work. Soll’s later criticisms of Skinner/Tuck are his own and are not assigned to Rodgers. Original1992 essay and Pocock’s books were not freshly read.

edges.relationship: As Soll explains, Rodgers points to Kerber’s social and cultural history as a resource for enlarging the study of republicanism beyond political language.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Soll2010,22/n6 attributes this methodological use to Rodgers1992,38,and jointly credits Rhys Isaac and Sean Wilentz. Their distinct work is not collapsed into Kerber’s or asserted as a shared school. Neither Rodgers’s original1992 ending nor the particular Kerber/Isaac/Wilentz works were freshly read; Soll does not identify individual work titles in this passage.

edges.relationship: As Richard J. Ross explains, Rodgers follows Williams’s keyword method while shifting attention toward the political uses and consequences of contested terms.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Ross1998,230,note1,contrasts genealogy with Rodgers’s forensic emphasis and points to Contested Truths(1987),3–16. The note cites Williams’s revised1983 Keywords; its historical edition is not silently changed. Only this substantive introductory note was read in a public reproduced/indexed extract; direct Yale retrieval returned403. Neither complete article nor Rodgers’s and Williams’s books were freshly read.

edges.relationship: Armitage identifies Yates’s Art of Memory as the book that inspired his wish to write cultural and intellectual history.
edges.evidence_note: Own retrospective account specifies a teenage reading and desired kind of history;not endorsement of every Yates thesis. First publication1966 and cited1978 reprint distinguished. The book itself remains unread.

edges.relationship: Armitage credits Skinner’s republicanism scholarship, supervision and sustained criticism with enabling his formation as an intellectual historian.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview identifies reading,matching republicanism interests and Cambridge transfer;own2000 acknowledgments separately name Skinner a reader,critic and interlocutor. No claim that administrative assistance alone proves doctrinal descent;Bock,Viroli and Russell Price retain the cited works’ editorial/translation credit. These works and dissertation remain unread.

edges.relationship: Armitage credits Pocock among his lasting intellectual inspirations during his Princeton fellowship.
edges.evidence_note: Own2000 acknowledgment expressly distinguishes Princeton inspiration from later Cambridge questions and examination. Elliott,Lake,Quint and the other Princeton colleague retain plural credit. This narrow self-reported formative debt identifies no particular doctrine,book or sole supervisor;their works remain unread.

edges.relationship: Armitage credits Stone among his lasting intellectual inspirations during his Princeton fellowship.
edges.evidence_note: Own2000 acknowledgment expressly distinguishes Princeton inspiration from later Cambridge questions and examination. Elliott,Lake,Quint and the other Princeton colleague retain plural credit. This narrow self-reported formative debt identifies no particular doctrine,book or sole supervisor;their works remain unread.

edges.relationship: Armitage credits Burke’s formative questions and support for a seminar connecting cultural and intellectual history with colonial encounters.
edges.evidence_note: Own2000 acknowledgment credits Burke with Bayly,Collinson,Hont and Pagden;own2012 account specifies support for Cultural Encounters in the Early-Modern World,which Armitage organized with Joan-Pau Rubiés. Neither sole supervision nor a particular question is inferred.

edges.relationship: Armitage describes his and Cannadine’s shared commitment to placing British history in imperial and wider international settings.
edges.evidence_note: Own2012 account says their views on the field converged while Cannadine was taking his own imperial turn. This is a bounded comparison,not a claim that collegial generosity proves intellectual transmission or that the NACBS report was jointly authored by them. Cannadine’s Ornamentalism remains unread.

edges.relationship: Armitage credits conversations with Iriye and other international historians with helping crystallize his turn toward international and global history.
edges.evidence_note: Own2012 retrospective singles out the2000/1 Warren Center conversations and jointly credits Ernest May and James Kloppenberg. The resource is this intellectual exchange,not an unspecified Iriye book or sole conversion cause. It coexisted with Atlantic work.

edges.relationship: Armitage explicitly acknowledges Bailyn’s expanding conception and seminars as an influence on his Atlantic historiography.
edges.evidence_note: Own2012 answer to the named-influence question describes annual seminar participation1997–2005 and historiographical innovation. This is Armitage’s own retrospective attribution,not inference from appearing at Harvard;his parallel international turn and criticism of nationally bounded Atlantic histories remain explicit.

edges.relationship: Armitage identifies domestic and short-term limits in Skinner’s contextualism while crediting its achievements and later expansion toward longer historical spans.
edges.evidence_note: Own2013 introduction3–4 specifies the international-actor omission,retaining the brief neo-Scholastic exception and period-wide context. Joint Guldi/Armitage2014,47–48,criticizes early synchronic narrowing but expressly credits Skinner’s late1990s longer-range studies as foreshadowing a broader return. Distinct qualified criticisms consolidate one pair/kind and coexist with acknowledged debt;neither all-contextualism rejection nor blanket claim about Skinner’s career follows. Skinner originals unread.

edges.relationship: Armitage and Jo Guldi build their renewed longue-durée program on Braudel’s model while revising its treatment of change and agency.
edges.evidence_note: Joint argument,not Armitage-only authorship. Frozen2October2014 PDF9–10 and15–17 distinguishes inheritance from a literal return;new data,flexibility and dynamism qualify the model. Braudel’s original1958 article/translation remain unread;later revised digital Manifesto is not substituted.

edges.relationship: Armitage and Guldi use Bourdieu’s account of stylistic returns to explain why a renewed longue durée differs from its earlier form.
edges.evidence_note: Joint2014 introduction explicitly applies this conceptual resource;no claim that Bourdieu advocated their historical program. The cited Field of Cultural Production essay remains unread.

edges.relationship: Armitage and Guldi draw on Eley’s account of the separation of local social histories from broader political and social explanation.
edges.evidence_note: Joint2014 chapter uses Eley’s retrospective account and contrasts his ambitions with the separation he describes. This is their use of A Crooked Line,not independent confirmation that social history failed or agreement with every Eley argument. Full original book unread.

edges.relationship: Armitage and Guldi use Ginzburg’s study of the benandanti as an example of microhistory operating across radically different temporal scales.
edges.evidence_note: Joint2014 concession explicitly resists making microhistory intrinsically incompatible with temporal depth. The cited Storia notturna1989 is distinguished from his earlier benandanti book;neither original is freshly read.

edges.relationship: Armitage and Guldi use Levi’s account of microhistory’s transformative capacity to qualify their criticism of its later anglophone practice.
edges.evidence_note: Joint2014 quotation and attribution retain individual agency within constraining normative systems. This does not make Levi responsible for the book’s diagnosis of anglophone microhistory or identify him with the later practice criticized. His1991 chapter remains unread;Peter Burke is volume editor.

edges.relationship: Armitage and Guldi use Hunt’s argument that the research question should determine scale to support synthesis between microhistory and macrohistory.
edges.evidence_note: Joint2014 conclusion explicitly endorses Hunt’s qualification that mega-long-term history is not the only story. It coexists with Hunt’s later criticism of their project;does not imply her endorsement of their whole program. Writing History in the Global Era2014,120 is cited but unread.

edges.relationship: Armitage and Guldi present James C. Scott’s Zomia history as an example of combining local histories into an account that challenges inevitable state and economic development.
edges.evidence_note: Joint2014 conclusion makes this specific methodological use of The Art of Not Being Governed2009. Scott’s historical claims are reported as their reading,not independently verified;no all-purpose influence or agreement is inferred. Original book unread.

edges.relationship: Hunt disputes Armitage and Guldi’s diagnosis of historical short-termism and their treatment of cultural history and microhistory as causes of disciplinary crisis.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh selected Portuguese translation by Danilo Alves Bezerra of Hunt’s2015 Annales response. Its direct target is their joint2015 Le retour de la longue durée article,not silently the whole2014 book. Hunt contests the data reading and treatment of Sewell,Davis,Darnton and Scott,and points to structural labor and educational changes;she also calls longue durée fruitful. French original and English edition were not read or paginated as this translation.

edges.relationship: Armitage and Guldi place Natalie Zemon Davis’s episodic cultural histories within their criticism of the narrowing horizons of anglophone microhistory.
edges.evidence_note: Joint2014 chapter names the works as examples while conceding microhistory’s original ability to link scales,public popularity and critical gains. This does not say the author’s entire career lacked public engagement. Hunt’s2015 response expressly disputes the characterization;her target is the related2015 article. The cited Davis1975/Darnton1984 books remain unread.

edges.relationship: Armitage and Guldi place Robert Darnton’s episodic cultural histories within their criticism of the narrowing horizons of anglophone microhistory.
edges.evidence_note: Joint2014 chapter names the works as examples while conceding microhistory’s original ability to link scales,public popularity and critical gains. This does not say the author’s entire career lacked public engagement. Hunt’s2015 response expressly disputes the characterization;her target is the related2015 article. The cited Davis1975/Darnton1984 books remain unread.

edges.relationship: Armitage and Guldi place Joan Scott’s early labor history within a shift toward locally focused history that they argue weakened broader historical synthesis.
edges.evidence_note: Joint2014 chapter50 names Glassworkers of Carmaux1974 alongside William Sewell,while conceding that close focus need not conflict with broad perspectives. This periodization critique is not rejection of Scott’s whole career. Hunt’s2015 reply disputes their treatment of Scott and emphasizes public interventions;the related2015 article itself remains unread.

edges.relationship: Armitage uses Weber’s analysis of charisma’s routinization and succession to suggest extensions to David A. Bell’s account of revolutionary leadership.
edges.evidence_note: Own2021 review distinguishes Bell’s historical development of relational charisma from Weber’s theoretical resource,and offers friendly chronological,geographical and analytical amendments. Bell is not an available endpoint. This records Armitage’s actual use of Weber,not an arrow inferred from Bell’s own debt. Original Weber texts and Bell’s full book unread.

edges.relationship: Armitage identifies the relation between charisma and race as a question left untreated by Weber’s account and Bell’s historical development of it.
edges.evidence_note: Own2021review8 explicitly identifies the dual lacuna while inviting future investigation. This bounded conceptual criticism coexists with Armitage’s productive use of Weber and praise of Bell. It does not claim independent collation of Weber’s complete works or make Bell a graph endpoint;Chateaubriand supplies a historical illustration,not scholarly coauthorship.

edges.relationship: Davis disputes Williams’s economic-decline explanation of British abolition while explicitly separating it from slavery’s contribution to industrialization.
edges.evidence_note: Own2012 reply to Barbara Solow, whose contrary evidence and defense remain explicit in the exchange. Davis limits his repudiation to the decline/abolition hypothesis and credits Williams for initiating the debate; his strong consensus language is his assessment, not the atlas’s final verdict. Williams1944, Ryden and the cited economic histories remain unread.

edges.relationship: Genovese’s analysis of slaveholding social relations and ideology supplies a resource in Davis’s account of slavery and abolition.
edges.evidence_note: Davis1995 explicitly finds the Genovese/Fox-Genovese case convincing; their credit remains shared. Sinha2019pp152–153 separately identifies Genovese’s influence on the1975 Age of Revolution and their conversations as fellows. Named mediation for that earlier transmission, not fresh reading of either1970s book. Sinha’s speculative reverse Hegel transmission is not accepted. This resource coexists with Davis’s specific1995criticism.

edges.relationship: Davis values Genovese’s recovery of Southern thought but questions his political alliance with conservatism and his treatment of the liberal tradition.
edges.evidence_note: Own1995review, concluding objection: Davis invokes liberal critics of human perfectibility and argues that dismantling public power can serve corporate interests. Praise of scholarship and shared concerns about market values remain explicit. These are Davis’s political/intellectual judgments about the three reviewed books, not an editorial judgment of Genovese’s whole career; books unread.

edges.relationship: Foner praises Davis’s trilogy but questions speculative psychological dehumanization and notes that the book’s fugitive-slave evidence challenges its generalization.
edges.evidence_note: Own2014review distinguishes racial dehumanization as a legal/social practice from claims of internalized psychological damage. Foner values Davis’s treatment of free Black leadership and contingency while making this objection. The criticism targets the2014volume’s argument; no dismissal of the trilogy or whole-book reading claimed.

edges.relationship: In Garrett Epps’s reading, Davis adapts Hofstadter’s paranoid-style concept to antebellum Slave Power arguments.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation, Epps2004p186, not fresh reading of Davis1969 or Hofstadter. Epps also criticizes Davis for conflating fringe conspiracy claims with sober constitutional arguments; his objection remains attributed and is held for missing Epps endpoint. A bounded conceptual resource, not endorsement of the diagnosis of abolitionists.

edges.relationship: Sinha identifies Weber’s Protestant Ethic as a model for Davis’s chapter on the Quaker ethic and antislavery international.
edges.evidence_note: Named Sinha2019reading atp153; she differentiates humble early Quaker dissenters from the later capitalist-elite emphasis and criticizes the latter. This is her identified model, not a primary Davis acknowledgment; Weber1905 and Davis1975chapter5 remain unread. No claim that Weber alone supplied the argument.

edges.relationship: Sinha reads Davis’s account of British antislavery’s social function as an application of Gramsci’s ideological-hegemony concept.
edges.evidence_note: Named Sinha2019p154 and note35(bookp379); she distinguishes Genovese’s slaveholder application, Davis’s British limit and Ashworth’s American extension while criticizing the explanatory consequences. Original Davis and Gramsci passages remain unread; no wholesale Marxist-school affiliation or agreement with Sinha inferred.

edges.relationship: Faust places Davis’s linking of ideas, institutions and social action among the slavery histories that redirected her generation’s research.
edges.evidence_note: Own2014review includes first-person recollection of1970sgraduate/early-career scholarship and names Davis prominently within a plural cohort. It supports an attributed scholarly resource, not sole mentoring, a fixed school, or a claim that every part of Faust’s work derives from Davis. Her later discussion is a review of Davis2014, not fresh reading of the trilogy.

edges.relationship: Davis adapts Freudian transference, through Erikson’s Gandhi’s Truth, as one explanation for metropolitan British concern with distant slavery.
edges.evidence_note: Explicitly mediated by Manisha Sinha (2019), p. 151/n. 25: she identifies Davis’s admiration for Erik H. Erikson’s 1969 book and his application of transference in Age of Revolution. Erikson retains the intermediary credit; no direct Freud reading or whole-book method is asserted. Sinha criticizes this psychological explanation; Foner separately criticizes a later Freudian excursion, without documenting the same transmission chain. Freud, Erikson and Davis originals remain unread.

edges.relationship: Morton argues that Creighton’s Laurentian narrative cannot unite Canada when it leaves Quebecers, easterners, westerners and working people outside its national ideal.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1979 address distinguishes the validity of Creighton’s account of Confederation from its limitations as a unifying myth. Own 2000 p. 19 returns to the restricted elite geography. This is Morton’s judgment, not a finding that Creighton’s original books were freshly read.

edges.relationship: Morton questions whether the limited-identities framework named by Careless can supply an adequate account of Canada as a whole without a new synthesis.
edges.evidence_note: The 1979 criticism targets fragmentation within a framework explicitly attributed to Careless; it is not a claim that Careless personally advocated every grievance Morton describes. Morton welcomes the framework’s insights, methods and wider participation, and his 2000 p. 19 praises its fit with diverse experience. Careless’s 1969 original remains unread.

edges.relationship: Morton credits Ramsay Cook, alongside David Kwavnick, for analysis of the Task Force on National Unity report used in his 1979 address.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit own acknowledgment in note 4. Preserve Kwavnick’s shared credit; no claim that Cook supplied the entire address, endorsed its conclusions or was Morton’s teacher.

edges.relationship: Morton questions whether Palmer’s Hamilton study substantiates its claims for working-class culture and historiographic novelty, while crediting its research on unions, conflict and politics.

Own 2000 pp. 23–25 revisits evidence and rhetoric, but p. 24 n. 50 says Palmer pp. 46–49 does not confirm Bercuson’s criticism. Bercuson, Ryerson, Armstrong and McNaught remain separate quoted critics, not Morton’s own original evidence. Complete Palmer books unread.

edges.relationship: Morton questions the duration and breadth of working-class unity in Kealey’s Toronto interpretation and the claimed departure from institutional and political labour history.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1983 pp. 175–178 praises Kealey’s book and recognizes his handling of sectarian complexity while questioning novelty and cultural transfer; own 2000 pp. 23–24 doubts that cross-sectarian unity lasted long. His 2000 pp. 25–27 credits the new historians’ durable empirical and regional gains. This is a distinct personal criticism already mediated in group edge 993, not removal or replacement of that qualified contribution.

edges.relationship: Morton adopts Hobsbawm’s injunction to combine historical interpretation with efforts to change the world, applying it to his own reformist labour history.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1983 and 2000 explicitly apply this purpose to nonrevolutionary historians including himself. Both cite Hobsbawm’s 1974 essay through Kealey and Peter Warrian’s 1976 Essays introduction; that intermediary credit remains. The original Hobsbawm essay is unread. Morton explicitly rejects revolutionary transformation in 2000 p. 13.

edges.relationship: Palmer supplies Morton with a practical prompt and a comparative-publication correction for his 2000 assessment of labour history.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2000 p. 12 identifies Palmer’s May 2000 review of Russell Jacoby’s The End of Utopia as the immediate intellectual prompt. Morton says this may not be what either author intended and distinguishes his reformism on p. 13. Palmer’s review and Jacoby’s book are unread; invitation to publish alone is not the basis. On p. 26/n. 57 Morton also credits Palmer’s 12 June 2000 letter for the comparison that Labour/Le Travail’s French-publication record was better than the Canadian Historical Review’s. The letter itself is unread; this is Morton’s printed report, not independent verification of its counts.

edges.relationship: Palmer describes Morton’s Working People as uneven in quality, a criticism Morton himself reports and partly concedes.
edges.evidence_note: Primary witness is Morton’s own 2000 p. 11/n. 2 quoting Palmer’s Working-Class Experience, second edition (1992), p. 418. Palmer’s original passage and the specific Working People edition it assesses remain unread/unconfirmed; no broader dismissal is inferred. Terry Copp retains credit for the 1980 work, while later Morton editions and Copp’s withdrawal are distinct.

edges.relationship: Morton disputes Granatstein’s claim that Canadian history had been killed, pointing to successful teaching and strong public interest.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2002 article explicitly names his friend and coauthor, then rejects the death diagnosis while acknowledging problems in teaching. Friendship and collaborative work do not establish agreement; Granatstein’s 1998 book remains unread.

edges.relationship: Morton and Granatstein’s joint war histories connect combat experience with industrialization, rationing and the wider effects of the world wars on Canadian society.
edges.evidence_note: Editorial comparison grounded in Tim Cook’s substantive 2003 review of their joint Canada and the Two World Wars. Cook identifies the two earlier books combined, praises integration and notes the bodies were not updated although the introduction is new. Joint authorship and reception do not establish intellectual influence or a division of labor. Full joint books unread.

edges.relationship: Morton notes that Parr’s Labouring Children necessarily reconstructs childhood largely through adult evidence, limiting recovery of children’s own voices.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2000 p. 33/n. 92 pairs Joy Parr’s Labouring Children (1980) with Neil Sutherland’s Children in English-Canadian Society (1976). Both retain credit; Morton calls the evidence limitation inevitable and places it within an otherwise positive assessment of feminist and family-history expansion. This is a qualified methodological limit, not rejection of Parr’s achievement or a claim to have read her full book.

edges.relationship: Owram praises Parr’s individual studies but questions whether Domestic Goods sustains a coherent argument about consumer sovereignty and the rationality of Canadian choices.
edges.evidence_note: Own2001 review103–105: distinguishes the restricted postwar market from later choices and consumers collectively from individual consumers. He credits Parr’s modernist-design and material-culture studies; disagreement is particular, not rejection of her work. The complete book remains unread.

edges.relationship: As Buckner reconstructs the1997 argument, Owram calls for studying how regional and local identities interact within a shared national experience while rejecting a return to a patriotic elite’s master narrative.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit Buckner2000 mediation, paragraphs10–15 and notes18/19. Buckner disputes Owram’s equation of regional study with overspecialization and qualifies common-law/social-program claims, while accepting his concluding focus on identity interplay. The original Narrow Circles remains unread. Do not collapse this position into Bliss’s or Granatstein’s.

edges.relationship: Faust uses Woodward’s burden-of-Southern-history framework while revising whose experiences it represents.
edges.evidence_note: Own1996 answer explicitly relates the framework to Mothers of Invention and her ending. The resource and her criticism coexist;no claim of personal supervision or adoption of all Woodward interpretations. His original essays and complete1996 book remain unread.

edges.relationship: Faust argues that Woodward’s burden-of-Southern-history account changes when examined through African Americans’ and white Southern women’s experiences.
edges.evidence_note: Own1996 interview says Woodward focuses on white Southern men and identifies her ending as taking issue with that emphasis. This is a particular representational qualification,not dismissal of Woodward’s entire career or claim that the two other groups share one historical burden.

edges.relationship: Faust identifies Genovese among the slavery scholars who redirected her early research and recalls his intellectual importance in the Southern Intellectual History Circle.
edges.evidence_note: Own2014 first-person account credits a plural cohort;own2023 retrospect recalls Genovese’s insights at meetings and explicitly assesses his account of ideology. Elizabeth Fox-Genovese retains intellectual and coauthor credit,especially for the later trilogy. This is a bounded scholarly resource,not sole mentoring or adherence to paternalism. Original books remain unread;2023 selected substantial indexed primary passages checked despite direct-page failures.

edges.relationship: Faust rejects Genovese’s paternalism framework while arguing that its disappearance leaves unresolved questions about slaveholders’ self-justifying ideas.

She retains his acknowledgment of cruelty,his later revisions,and the problem of ideology that remains after rejection. Elizabeth Fox-Genovese is coauthor of the later master-class studies;criticism does not assign those books to Eugene alone or equate understanding enslavers with endorsement. Complete original books unread.

edges.relationship: Faust uses Johnson’s challenge to paternalism to explain how the slave market unsettled accounts of reciprocal master–slave obligations.

It is not agreement with every claim of the later New History of Capitalism;her separate criticism of that approach remains. Johnson’s original book/articles and Tadman’s original research were not read.

edges.relationship: Faust questions whether the New History of Slavery’s Capitalism,including Johnson’s work,adequately explains slaveholders’ ideas and regional cultural differences.

Baptist and Jones-Rogers are separate,more individually detailed examples;their specific claims are not reassigned to this target. edges.relationship: Morgan uses Pocock’s reconstruction of republican political ideas to explain the connection between property,independence and liberty in Jefferson’s outlook.

edges.relationship: Morgan credits Davis’s research suggestions while using his work to examine how opposition to African slavery could coexist with demands to enslave the idle poor.

This records specific scholarly assistance and a textual resource,not the inference that Davis invented Morgan’s whole Virginia mechanism. The original Davis and Hutcheson works remain unread.

edges.relationship: Morgan uses Tawney’s New Medicine for Poverty formulation to interpret religious discipline and republican distrust of the idle poor.
edges.evidence_note: Own1972p10 names Tawney’s formulation within the argument connecting freedom,dependency and prescribed coerced labor. This selected passage supplies no exact original Tawney work/edition;none is guessed and the original remains unread.

edges.relationship: Morgan places Weber’s interpretation of disciplined religious conduct within his explanation of republican attitudes toward poverty and compulsory labor.

Original Weber work/edition not specified in this passage and unread.

edges.relationship: Morgan uses Bailyn’s reconstruction of Commonwealthman ideas to explain the development of revolutionary American political thought.

edges.relationship: Morgan argues that Bailyn’s sympathetic Hutchinson biography risks understating the revolutionaries’ justified fears of arbitrary power.

He points to patronage and unlimited Parliamentary authority as real dangers. This qualified criticism does not deny ideological fear or endorse Hutchinson’s persecution;it is distinct from the existing Morgan→Bailyn contribution.

edges.relationship: Morgan uses Berlin’s negotiated-relationship account of slavery to argue for understanding enslaved people’s cultural autonomy without reducing them to passive victims.
edges.evidence_note: Own1998review explicitly builds this argument through Many Thousands Gone while also crediting Philip D.Morgan’s distinct Slave Counterpoint. Joint Edmund/MarieMorgan2010review again uses Berlin’s synthesis of family,culture and migration. This is a particular interpretive resource,not an assertion that Berlin originated every agency argument or that negotiation implied equal bargaining power. edges.relationship: Morgan qualifies Berlin’s reconstruction of slave culture and the presentation of testimony,questioning unsupported attributions and the risk that guilt obscures agency.
edges.evidence_note: Own1998review distinguishes two targets:Many Thousands Gone’s African-origin/oppositional attributions may outrun sparse sources,yet its framework is praised;Remembering Slavery’s presentation may invite guilt/pity,yet the closing Faulk recollection is a corrective. Marc Favreau and Steven F.Miller share collection editing,not sole-authored Many Thousands Gone. Dialect/audio presentation is part of the latter criticism. WGBH productions are separate targets. These are Morgan’s contested interpretive judgments;original books/audio unread.

edges.relationship: Edmund and Marie Morgan use Woodward’s account of Jim Crow’s development in interpreting the timing and pressures of African-American migration.

The review’s chronology is their reading,not independently verified here;no claim that this exhausts Woodward’s account or that Berlin’s whole argument derives from him. The original Woodward work is unnamed in the selected passage and unread.

edges.relationship: May identifies Gordon’s women’s-history scholarship as an influence on her early research and her understanding of the connections between public and private life.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2025 retrospective explicitly names Gordon among a plural peer cohort and cites Woman’s Body, Woman’s Right (1976) in note 7. This is May’s later recollection, not proof that a 1976 book shaped her 1975 degree work. The cited original is unread. Gordon is a peer/inspiration here, not an inferred formal supervisor. May also gives world events a larger role in prompting her questions.

edges.relationship: May credits Kerber’s women’s-history scholarship as an early research influence and uses republican motherhood to explain the older civic lineage of Cold War domestic ideals.

No 1980-to-1975 causal chronology, sole-source claim or formal mentorship inferred. Complete Kerber original and Homeward Bound endnote 28 remain unread.

edges.relationship: May draws on Roediger’s account of Irish immigrants’ pursuit of whiteness when explaining changing racial boundaries and postwar mobility.
edges.evidence_note: Own PBS answer explicitly credits Roediger, then differentiates later immigrant cohorts and enduring exclusions. The interview does not identify which Roediger work or edition; no title is guessed and no original book is newly read. This extends the source’s previously checked employment/family passages with an explicit named conceptual resource.

edges.relationship: May’s review endorses Cott’s account of marriage law as a constitutive part of citizenship, racial and gender hierarchy, and national policy.

Cott’s 2000 Public Vows and the remainder of May’s pp. 1046–1047 review are unread.

This is a specific conceptual use within a speculative private reflection, not proof of his whole fascism interpretation or endorsement of his empirical/political generalizations. Quinn’s note 33 cites a 2000 revised edition of The Civilizing Process; that later editorial reference is not the edition Weber read in 1981. Original manuscript and Elias book unread.

edges.relationship: Weber uses the Tillys’ distinction between local protest and national political action to test claims about peasant politicization in 1848–1851.

All three retain credit. No agreement with their entire theory or direct reading of the complete 1975 book is asserted. A separate Tilly criticism of Weber coexists.

edges.relationship: Tilly challenges Weber’s image of an isolated traditional countryside transformed after 1870, emphasizing earlier markets, class divisions and national politics.

Michael Burns’s 1984 p. 5 independently and substantively attributes this criticism and Tilly’s alternative emphasis on capitalism/state-making. Burns’s original is successfully available locally; precise later published Tilly chapter wording is not presumed identical to the draft. Tilly praises Weber’s ethnographic richness while disputing the model; Weber’s complete 1976 book and Tilly’s later chapter remain unread.

edges.relationship: Judt uses Weber’s account of interwar decline and insecurity to establish the prewar background of Vichy and postwar France.

Judt’s criticism of Miller is not assigned to Weber. This is identifiable argumentative use, not formative influence or agreement with every Weber interpretation. Full Weber book unread.

edges.relationship: Uses Ricœur’s account of memory, historical explanation and narrative to articulate the historian’s work and its civic responsibilities.
edges.evidence_note: Own2011 answer finds Ricœur’s three event strata operational; own2017 positive exposition76–79 supports the particular resource. Own2012 retrospective discovery of agreement during Structuralism research precedes biography and later personal contact; friendship or biography alone is not treated as influence. Full original works unread.

edges.relationship: Recalls reading and commenting on chapters of Memory, History, Forgetting and guiding Ricœur through historiographical work, especially Certeau.

His account says the intellectual biography preceded their meetings and that Ricœur then sent chapters for corrections. edges.evidence_note: Own2011 qualified objection to this specific reading in Memory, History, Forgetting, alongside substantial agreement with Ricœur. Does not make hostility or reject his philosophy wholesale. The original exchange in Le Débat and complete books unread.

edges.relationship: Uses Certeau’s historiographical operation and attention to singular cases and the historian’s position to develop a reflexive history.
edges.evidence_note: Own2011 answer explicitly values marginal cases and own2012 attributes reflexive inscription to Certeau.2017 Certeau passages partly explain Ricœur’s use rather than a separate firsthand encounter. Dosse explicitly says he never met Certeau; no personal mentorship inferred.

edges.relationship: Uses Nora’s lieux de mémoire to treat changing traces and appropriations of the past as objects of historical inquiry.
edges.evidence_note: Own2011 discussion identifies a methodological opening across periods, reinforced in2012 and2017 conclusion. This is specific analytical use, not a resource inferred merely because Dosse wrote Nora’s biography. The complete original collective work unread. Own2012 additionally recalls Nora supplying crucial details during biographical research under an agreement to maintain distance; this bounded informant contribution is consolidated here, not a claim Nora controlled or endorsed the finished book.

edges.relationship: Uses Hartog’s regimes of historicity and presentism to diagnose an obscured future and the expansion of memorial demands.
edges.evidence_note: Own2011 explicitly adopts Hartog’s hypothesis and own2017 attributes the conceptual diagnosis at68/72. No general pupil relation, no historical inevitability, and no current legal claim. Original Hartog books unread.

edges.relationship: Uses Bloch’s distinction between historical inquiry and judicial sentencing to argue for understanding rather than verdicts.

edges.relationship: Draws on Ginzburg’s evidentiary reasoning and Menocchio study to connect proof with singular cases that unsettle broad social categories.
edges.evidence_note: Two particular uses: own2011 microhistory argument and own2017 judge/historian discussion. Dosse’s2011 apparent Friuli dating is not certified or propagated. Notes7–8 identify1980 Signes and1997 French Le juge et l’historien; originals unread, not collapsed into one book.

edges.relationship: Invokes Febvre’s criticism of official national history and account of historical construction to defend critical inquiry.

A separate1932 lecture is mentioned at75. These originals unread; no claim that quoted formulas alone establish formal training.

edges.relationship: Treats Le dimanche de Bouvines as a methodological opening toward the changing memorial traces of an event.

edges.relationship: Uses Foucault’s Pierre Rivière case as an example of a singular history that exposes conflicts between medical and juridical authority.
edges.evidence_note: Own2011 specific positive example within his argument for singular cases; co-workers in the collective Rivière publication are not erased or treated as Dosse’s teachers. Original collective case study unread. This does not rely on the problematic ancient-sexuality illustration at2017 p69.

Pinagot book and complete Dosse book unread; loose interview language about absent archives is not certified as a literal no-evidence claim.

edges.relationship: Rejects Braudel’s reported dismissal of events in favor of a history that takes actors and singular situations seriously.

edges.evidence_note: Own2011 paragraph17 credits Cadres sociaux and Mémoire collective; follows it with a qualification against radical separation. This specific appropriation is not a formal genealogy or a statement of agreement with every consequence. Complete originals unread.

edges.evidence_note: Own2011 qualified interpretation: Dosse says if one pushes Halbwachs’s thought to its ultimate consequences, history begins when memory ends. Preserve that modal attribution rather than present it as a direct absolute quotation or reject Halbwachs’s entire work.

edges.relationship: Uses the Wilson biography attributed to Freud as a negative example of biographical hostility to its subject.
edges.evidence_note: Own2012 brief but explicit methodological judgment, contrasting empathy with a biography he considers unsuccessful. The work is coauthored with William C. Bullitt, not Freud alone; bibliographic coauthor credit checked against Routledge publisher record, https://www.routledge.com/link/link/p/book/9781138540705 (copyright1966). No complete original or general rejection of psychoanalysis claimed.

edges.relationship: Invokes Lévi-Strauss’s bricolage as an analogy for the singular construction of Menocchio’s culture.
edges.evidence_note: Own2011 paragraph34 describes Ginzburg’s Menocchio through this named conceptual analogy. This establishes the particular use, not direct reading of a specified Lévi-Strauss text or formal mentorship; complete original works unread. Claude Lévi-Strauss is distinct from Giovanni Levi.

edges.relationship: Applies Freudian categories of repression, return and obsession to the changing forms of collective memory.
edges.evidence_note: Own2011 paragraph22 explicitly endorses this conceptual use after discussing Rousso, Joutard and Stora as historical examples. These named mediations remain; no direct reading of a particular Freud text or general equation of individual and collective processes is certified. Coexists with his distinct negative2012 judgment of the Wilson biography.

edges.relationship: Hartog credits Certeau’s reading of Jean de Léry with shaping his questions about Herodotus and otherness, and Certeau’s challenge about unthought historical time with prompting his later temporal inquiry.

Hartog recalls the stimulus before1975;editorial note8 identifies the1975collection text,not proof of an earlier book edition. No exclusive genealogy or complete Certeau/Herodotus reading claimed. This second retrospective prompt is consolidated in the same influence pair; it establishes no exclusive origin or original Certeau text collation.

edges.relationship: Hartog credits his reading of Lévi-Strauss with an anthropological openness that helped reframe his relation to ancient Greece.

It does not identify a particular Lévi-Strauss work or make travel the sole cause;no title/edition is guessed and originals remain unread.

edges.relationship: Hartog identifies Braudel’s writings on history as a resource for his own historiography teaching and reflection.

edges.relationship: Hartog uses Koselleck’s tension between experience and expectation to formulate the problem of presentism.

Note29 cites a2006edition without a matching complete bibliography entry;original edition/work not guessed and unread.

edges.relationship: Hartog uses Arendt’s image of a gap in time to explore whether presentism represents a pause or a more durable regime.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview363 explicitly borrows the image while retaining uncertainty about its application. Editorial note28 points to a1961reference and Portuguese rendering,but supplies no complete matching bibliographic entry;no original edition or whole Arendt theory is invented. Original text unread.

edges.relationship: Hartog uses Ricœur’s inquiries into narrative,time and historical representation as a resource for reflecting on historians’ own practice.
edges.evidence_note: Own2012answer360 credits Ricœur’s actual reading of historians;369identifies contemporary interpreters as sources for his reflection.
