It coexists with a later objection about Aristotle’s Rhetoric;not whole-program agreement or formative mentoring. Cited French2003Rapports de force and2010Le fil et les traces remain unread.

edges.relationship: Hartog questions whether Ginzburg’s linkage of rhetoric and proof establishes Aristotle’s Rhetoric as the primary ancient account of historiography.
edges.evidence_note: Own2011/2013article20–21 examines Thucydides’ reconstruction of the remote past and Aristotle’s placement of inquiries within political deliberation. Hartog grants the importance of proof and Ginzburg’s narrative sophistication;his objection is a particular ancient-text interpretation,not equating realism with positivism. Original Ginzburg works and Greek-text editions not freshly read beyond Hartog’s translated quotations.

edges.relationship: Hartog argues that Ricœur’s extension of Aristotelian emplotment to historical narrative crosses the Poetics’ original separation of history from poetry.
edges.evidence_note: Own2011/2013article21–22 calls this extension Ricœur’s philosophical right and recognizes his effort to preserve history’s referential intention through representance. It is a bounded interpretive disagreement,not accusation of fabrication or denial of Ricœur’s wider value. The negative effect of later historians’ deference is explicitly not assigned to Ricœur himself.

edges.relationship: Hartog argues that White’s incorporation of historical poetics into rhetoric moves beyond Aristotle’s exclusion of history from poetic mimesis.
edges.evidence_note: Own2011/2013article18–19 identifies the interpretive move while carefully distinguishing Ricœur’s and Ginzburg’s different readings of White. This is Hartog’s limited ancient/modern conceptual qualification,not wholesale rejection of narrative analysis or attribution of every anti-White argument to him. Metahistory and White’s complete corpus unread.

edges.relationship: Hartog challenges the transhistorical authority claimed by Veyne’s invariant-based method and asks where the historian’s own discourse is produced.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh1978primary essay read in Gustavo Ruiz Da Silva’s2025English translation,especially Without Concepts,You Don’t See Anything. It interrogates the relation of invariant models to progress in knowledge and likens classification to a herbarium. OriginalFrench326–327metadata/selectedOCR checked,but key329–330not obtained;no complete French-original reading claimed. Translator’s historical introduction/bracketed additions are distinct;Veyne’s1977lecture unread.

edges.relationship: Hartog uses Foucault’s analysis of classical classification to develop his criticism of Veyne’s invariant method.
edges.evidence_note: Own1978essay,read in2025translation,explicitly refers to Les mots et les choses together with François Jacob’s La logique du vivant as the source of the closing natural-history quotations and analogy. Jacob retains separate credit;they are two works,not coauthors. Neither original work nor its exact edition was freshly read;translator commentary is not used as Hartog’s argument.

edges.relationship: Bederman explicitly credits Foucault’s discourse analysis with shaping her study of knowledge, material practice and power, while stressing contradiction and possible agency.
edges.evidence_note: Own methodological declaration at printed24, followed by three specified uses of discourse analysis on24–25. Note97 identifies The History of Sexuality, vol.1 and Power/Knowledge; note29 also includes the former. No exclusive genealogy, agreement with every Foucauldian position or independent reading of Foucault’s originals. Note97 prints an unverified1972 date for Power/Knowledge; this is not silently adopted as an edition fact.

edges.relationship: Bederman includes Butler’s Gender Trouble among the theoretical resources for treating gender as a historical process connecting bodies, identities and authority.
edges.evidence_note: Body7 develops an ideological-process account; note29 directs readers first to Teresa de Lauretis and then, among plural resources, to Butler1990, Foucault1978, Denise Riley1988 and Scott1988/1992. A bounded, explicitly cited conceptual resource; not a claim of personal mentoring, sole derivation or full adoption. Original Gender Trouble unread.

edges.relationship: Bederman includes Scott’s gender-history and experience writings among the theoretical resources for her historical account of gender and authority.
edges.evidence_note: Body7/n29 names Gender and the Politics of History (1988) and Experience in Feminists Theorize the Political (1992), edited jointly by Judith Butler and Scott,22–40. De Lauretis, Butler, Foucault and Riley retain co-credit. This is use of a particular theoretical bibliography, not proof that Bederman adopted all Scott’s arguments; cited originals unread.

edges.relationship: Bederman credits Higginbotham’s analysis of race and gender among recent theoretical discussions informing the intersection she investigates.
edges.evidence_note: At5 Bederman explicitly adopts Hazel Carby’s call to interrogate racial specificity and whiteness. Note23 also identifies Higginbotham’s African-American Women’s History and the Metalanguage of Race, together with Berger/Brown/Hewitt and Lerner, as important recent theoretical discussions. This plural, bounded historiographic resource does not replace the more direct Carby credit or imply exclusive derivation. Higginbotham original unread; no guessed correction of the date as printed in Bederman’s note.

edges.relationship: Bederman draws on Ryan’s Cradle of the Middle Class to connect early middle-class formation, manly self-restraint and gendered family practices.
edges.evidence_note: Body11–12 with notes38–40/43–44 explicitly supports these historical explanations. Davidoff and Hall’s joint Family Fortunes is credited alongside Ryan; Blumin, Paul E. Johnson and Cott supply other aspects. No independent collation of Ryan1981 or wholesale adoption of her account.

edges.relationship: Bederman uses Davidoff and Hall’s jointly authored Family Fortunes for the place of manliness and gendered family practices in middle-class formation.
edges.evidence_note: Note38 expressly judges some observations from the English study applicable to the United States; body11–12 and notes40/42–43 use that joint work alongside Ryan, Cott and others. Both coauthors retain equal credit. This is a qualified transatlantic resource, not an assertion that English and American class formation were identical. Family Fortunes (1987) unread independently.

edges.relationship: Bederman uses Davidoff and Hall’s jointly authored Family Fortunes for the place of manliness and gendered family practices in middle-class formation.
edges.evidence_note: Note38 expressly judges some observations from the English study applicable to the United States; body11–12 and notes40/42–43 use that joint work alongside Ryan, Cott and others. Both coauthors retain equal credit. This is a qualified transatlantic resource, not an assertion that English and American class formation were identical. Family Fortunes (1987) unread independently.

edges.relationship: Bederman uses Cott’s histories of womanhood and feminism in explaining gendered middle-class identity and challenges to established male authority.
edges.evidence_note: Body11/n40 cites The Bonds of Womanhood (1977) alongside Ryan and jointly authored Davidoff/Hall;14/n53 cites The Grounding of Modern Feminism (1987) with Mari Jo Buhle and Filene. Note96 also points to Cott’s Two Beards (1990) as another discussion of civilization, without making that a personal formative claim. Cott originals unread.

edges.relationship: Bederman uses Higham’s accounts of nativism and cultural reorientation as resources for connecting white middle-class manhood to immigrant politics and the appeal of boxing.
edges.evidence_note: Body13/n50 links immigrant contests for city government to power and manhood, citing Strangers in the Land (1971 consulted edition) with Gossett. Body17/n72 cites Reorientation,78–79 for boxing’s wider middle-class attraction. This scoped use coexists with her criticism of a masculinity-crisis formulation; it is not evidence of complete agreement. Originals unread.

edges.relationship: Bederman qualifies the masculinity-crisis interpretation represented in part by Higham, arguing that ongoing change and contradictory authority claims do not by themselves establish a crisis of male identity or power.
edges.evidence_note: Body10–11 acknowledges merit in both crisis and domesticity interpretations, then distinguishes remaking gender from evidence that men lost confidence in male identity and authority. Note36 names Higham’s Reorientation alongside Dubbert, Filene, Kimmel and McGovern; note37 credits Marsh and Griffen’s corrective. A bounded collective criticism, not rejection of all Higham’s work; her separate uses of his nativism and boxing discussions remain.

edges.relationship: Bederman uses Roediger’s Wages of Whiteness in explaining how white working men linked manly independence to exclusion of Black men.
edges.evidence_note: Body20/n84 supports the specific contrast between white male claims to independence and exclusions shared by women and Black men. The note identifies Roediger1991; nearby Berthoff and Horton/Horton discussions have distinct claims. No independent reading of Wages of Whiteness or inference of personal affiliation.

edges.relationship: Bederman cites Lears’s account of neurasthenia among the resources for explaining anxieties about allegedly depleted white middle-class male vitality.
edges.evidence_note: Body14/n54 uses No Place of Grace (1981),49–57 with Gosling, the jointly authored Haller study, Rotundo and Lutz, alongside contemporary George Beard. This is a specific plural resource, not an exclusive origin for the book’s argument or an endorsement of the historical disease categories. The Lears original remains unread.

edges.relationship: Bederman includes Hofstadter’s Social Darwinism in American Thought among the historiographic resources for her account of Darwinism’s American reception and its tensions with Protestant millennial expectations.
edges.evidence_note: Body26 describes educated Americans understanding Darwinism through conflict and survival without the older providential telos. Note102 directs readers to Hofstadter’s1955 edition alongside Robert C. Bannister1979 and Cynthia Eagle Russett1976 for Darwinism’s reception in the United States. This is a particular plural historical resource, not personal formation or wholesale adoption of Hofstadter’s interpretation. Originals unread. The separate self-employment statistic at12/n45 carries no additional interpretive claim.

edges.relationship: Wood questions Morgan’s emphasis on assigning responsibility and recovering the revolutionaries’ declared constitutional motives.
edges.evidence_note: Own1966 essay treats Morgan and Jack P. Greene as named examples of neo-Whig limits while calling restoration of the importance of ideas necessary and refreshing. It argues that judging motives and responsibility misses unintended processes and some emotional beliefs. This is qualified methodological criticism, not dismissal of Morgan’s scholarship. Original journal scan checked; no attribution of later reprint annotations to1966.

edges.relationship: Morgan accepts Wood’s social-revolution thesis while questioning his magnification of changes in labor, royal patronage and loyalist departures.
edges.evidence_note: Signed1992 review distinguishes persuasive central interpretation from overstated detail. Morgan invokes earlier Protestant valuation of work and the limited extent of royal patronage, and ends by endorsing the egalitarian transformation. Wood’s entire Radicalism was not read; no claim of blanket rejection.

edges.relationship: Wood questions Greene’s concentration on conscious constitutional motives and later psychological explanations of the American Revolution.
edges.evidence_note: Own1966 critique of neo-Whig historical explanation names Greene alongside Morgan, with necessary corrective credit retained. Own1982 opening identifies Greene’s Search for Identity1970 and Uneasy Connection1973 as examples of psychological readings that Wood seeks to replace with a wider account of eighteenth-century causal beliefs. Neither claim means every Greene interpretation was rejected.

edges.relationship: Wood uses Greene’s account of colonial legislative independence when reconstructing Americans’ experience of divided authority.
edges.evidence_note: Own2011 review credits Greene’s prominence and uses his account of colonial and Irish legislatures. Wood simultaneously argues that earlier local arrangements require more attention. The p707 description partly quotes LaCroix’s presentation of Greene; independent use at710/n13 makes the resource specific. Greene’s books and LaCroix’s full monograph unread; no formative influence claim.

edges.relationship: Wood borrows Pocock’s formulation of a Namierian history of ideas to characterize Bailyn’s analysis of revolutionary thought.
edges.evidence_note: Own1966 applies a specifically credited analytical formulation across the21–22 page break, n41 citing Pocock’s1965 articlep550. This is a small conceptual resource, not evidence that Wood adopted the whole later republican synthesis or a claim that Pocock coined every underlying idea. Pocock’s original article unread.

edges.relationship: Wood questions the explanatory limits and fixed republican categories of Pocock’s synthesis.
edges.evidence_note: Own1985 review of Diggins distinguishes Pocock’s synthesis from Diggins’s polemic. Wood questions its account of liberal America and objects to rigid categories, while recognizing its impact. He also reports Pocock’s self-qualification. Full Pocock and Diggins books unread.

edges.relationship: Wood uses Hofstadter’s description of conspiratorial explanation as personal causation to develop his own historical account.
edges.evidence_note: Own1982 essay explicitly takes up Hofstadter’s account of deliberate individual will when analyzing eighteenth-century causal assumptions. This conceptual use coexists with a challenge to its application across periods. Wood preserves possible modern applicability at his conclusion; full Hofstadter book unread.

edges.relationship: Wood challenges extending Hofstadter’s pathological and marginal model to widespread eighteenth-century beliefs.
edges.evidence_note: Own1982 distinguishes Hofstadter’s expressly metaphorical usage from clinical diagnosis and acknowledges that Hofstadter omitted the Revolution. Wood argues that contemporary rational causality made conspiratorial beliefs broadly intelligible, while allowing a different modern assessment at441. This is a contextual limit, not rejection of all Hofstadter’s analysis.

edges.relationship: Wood questions Davis’s linkage of revolutionary experience to a recurring American pattern of conspiratorial fear.
edges.evidence_note: Own1982p405 identifies Davis’s question about revolutionary national identity; Wood’s following alternative relocates such thinking in wider eighteenth-century causal assumptions. He calls Davis meticulous and retains Davis’s warning against reducing every fear to internal psychology at404. This qualifies the explanatory framing; it does not accuse Davis of clinical diagnosis or reject his whole slavery history.

edges.relationship: Wood questions Taylor’s treatment of captive violence and the narrative scale of The Divided Ground while praising its research and cultural analysis.
edges.evidence_note: Own2006 review distinguishes omission criticism from praise of the murder-law analysis and research. Richter supplies Wood’s captive-treatment counterexample; the approved Richter→Wood resource is separately represented, not repeated. Richter’s unnamed study remains bibliographically unidentified. Taylor’s complete book and later2016/2021reviews unread; no general verdict on Native history adopted.

edges.relationship: Wood objects that Turner’s1895 account of American origins leaves Indigenous people outside its historical explanation.
edges.evidence_note: Own2006 review singles out Turner’s first-issue AHR essay and contrasts it with later histories treating Indigenous people as participants. This is Wood’s criticism of a specified older text, not direct re-reading of Turner’s essay or a claim about every work Turner wrote.

edges.relationship: Wood uses Bailyn’s reconstruction of revolutionary ideas to frame a return to questions about their social sources.
edges.evidence_note: Own1966pp20–24treats Bailyn’s1965Pamphlets introduction as a departure toward social explanation, rather than merely conscious motivation. This concrete use of a published interpretation differs from baseline edge1775’s1958seminar teaching influence; no second influence edge. Original1965introduction unread; later1967book/reprint annotations not projected into1966.

edges.relationship: Wood invokes Arendt’s account of joint action to support his distinction between collective revolutionary processes and individual motives.
edges.evidence_note: Own1966p23/n44adds Arendt, On Revolution(NewYork1963),p173 to a paragraph principally explaining Bailyn’s interpretation. Her specified collective-action argument reinforces the point; Bailyn retains the main interpretive credit. This is a bounded conceptual contribution, not formative influence or a reading of Arendt’s complete book. Original1963text unread.

edges.relationship: Gellner uses Ibn Khaldun’s dynastic-cycle model to interpret the coexistence of tribal and urban power in Morocco.
edges.evidence_note: Own1961review explicitly applies the analysis rather than merely praising a precursor. Alatas2006p789also identifies a later fusion with Hume in Gellner’s Muslim reform model; Hume retains separate credit, not an Ibn-only explanation. No precise Muqaddimah edition for Gellner’s1961reading is established; originalArabic and complete Muslim Society unread.

edges.relationship: Malešević reports Gellner’s geographical qualification of Ibn Khaldun’s model to arid-zone tribal Islam.
edges.evidence_note: Named mediation: Malešević2021p394attributes the regional limit and quotes Muslim Society1981p88. His own following argument about modern conditions is kept separate. Gellner’s admiration and application coexist with this qualification. Original1981page and whole book unread; no generalized rejection of Ibn Khaldun.

edges.relationship: Gellner contrasts Khaldunian dynastic cycles with a Marxian account of colonial capitalism while arguing that both patterns coexist in Morocco.
edges.evidence_note: Own1961comparison, not a claim that Marx inherited the model. Gellner’s two historical frameworks coexist rather than one simply replacing the other. His interpretation is attributed; neither all Marx nor the full Muqaddimah was read.

edges.relationship: Gellner and Dale compare Ibn Khaldun with Durkheim on social cohesion and the explanatory study of society, retaining differences in context and normative aims.
edges.evidence_note: Gellner’s1975opening extract and Dale’s2006pp442–444supply distinct comparisons. Dale emphasizes shared logical methods and divergent historical conditions. This is their comparison; no direct transmission or medieval membership in modern sociology inferred. Full Durkheim works unread.

edges.relationship: Dale compares Ibn Khaldun and Bloch on cohesion, comparison and testing historical reports, while distinguishing Bloch’s attention to individual motives.
edges.evidence_note: Dale2006pp444–445reads Feudal Society and Historian’s Craft comparatively. Shared analytical questions do not establish direct reading or descent. Dale qualifies the analogy; complete Bloch works and underlying editions unread here.

edges.relationship: Dale compares Ibn Khaldun’s explanatory structure with Braudel’s layered historical times, while questioning the similarity’s logical depth.
edges.evidence_note: Dale2006p445and451n100explicitly distinguish analogy from intellectual contact: The Mediterranean does not mention Ibn Khaldun. Later cyclical-theory references are reported as a separate lead. No direct influence asserted; complete Braudel works unread.

edges.relationship: Dale reports White’s concern that Ibn Khaldun’s structural explanation can subordinate human action to underlying regularities.
edges.evidence_note: Mediated narrowly through Dale2006p444and450n92, which attributes the antihumanistic assessment of Ibn Khaldun to White’s1959review. Dale’s broader comparison is his own. Original review body unavailable; publisher extract/metadata only checked, including Rosenthal1958translation reviewed. No claim to reproduce White’s full evaluation or his later narrative theory.

edges.relationship: Hannoum compares Ibn Khaldun’s account of social status and wealth with Bourdieu’s economy of symbolic goods.
edges.evidence_note: Named2026comparison, separated from Hannoum’s further assertions of influence and reliance on colonial Algerian scholarship. The specific resemblance does not establish direct borrowing, a shared complete theory or a verified priority claim. Neither recipient original nor the Arabic passage was independently read; exact book/page references for this particular comparison are not supplied in the checked paragraph.

edges.relationship: Challenges McPherson’s portrayal of the Freedmen Project as a self-emancipation orthodoxy that excludes Lincoln.
edges.evidence_note: Own scanned essay29–33 calls this a caricature while acknowledging Lincoln’s centrality. Enslaved people are prime movers, not sole movers; citizens, soldiers, legislators and president retain distinct agency. Freedom, Free at Last and later volumes have collective editorial credit, including Barbara Jeanne Fields, Thavolia Glymph, Steven Miller, Joseph Reidy, Leslie Rowland and Julie Saville. Original McPherson paper and documentary volumes unread.

edges.relationship: As reported by Berlin, criticizes Berlin and the Freedmen Project for advancing a self-emancipation orthodoxy at Lincoln’s expense.
edges.evidence_note: Explicitly Berlin’s attributed reconstruction of McPherson’s1992 AHA paper, printed28–29, not fresh reading of McPherson’s text. Robert Engs and Vincent Harding are co-targets; critique is not aimed at Berlin alone. Berlin contests the characterization and affirms complementary agency, a reply retained in the separate reverse edge. McPherson’s complete published versions unread.

edges.relationship: Uses Hofstadter’s bill-of-lading characterization as a rhetorical foil in discussing the Emancipation Proclamation.
edges.evidence_note: Own scanned1996 essay30 reuses the attributed description;2001 Q&A qualifies its implication by emphasizing extraordinary effects despite flat wording. The speech calls it moral impact, whereas scanned essay says moral grandeur; do not silently merge as a verified original quotation. Original Hofstadter passage unread. This resource does not imply agreement that proclamation lacked political force.

edges.relationship: Identifies Davis’s slavery studies as guides to slavery’s double status as property and person and to abolition in the age of capitalism.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit authorial Prologue notes5–6 in displayed digital selection, with Hegel credited first in note5. Western Culture1966 and Age of Revolution1975 have distinct purposes. No direct first-edition collation or complete Prologue/book reading, and no general mentorship or causal debt inferred.

edges.relationship: Identifies Roll, Jordan, Roll as the starting point for the contemporary debate on master-slave paternalism.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit evaluative authorial note6 in displayed digital notes; a resource for a debate, not assent to all of Genovese’s conclusions. Coexists with Berlin’s particular2003 chronological-scope criticism.1974 title/year are as cited by Berlin; the2001 speech reading list uses a different1976 edition. Both original editions and full Berlin Prologue unread.

edges.relationship: Points to The Black Atlantic as a larger Atlantic perspective for understanding the formation of Black culture.
edges.evidence_note: Own PartI note2 explicitly characterizes this resource; preceding co-credited Linebaugh/Rediker and Thornton works have different roles. Only selected authorial digital notes read, not the continuous chapter or original Gilroy book. No automatic founding or personal mentorship claim.

edges.relationship: Questions the limited attention to slavery before1830 in Genovese’s nineteenth-century-centered historiography.
edges.evidence_note: Only the fresh publisher opening extract of Berlin2003 article read. He groups Genovese with Kenneth Stampp, Stanley Elkins, John Blassingame, Robert Fogel and Stanley Engerman and acknowledges their sharp disagreements. Do not infer rejection of paternalism, statistics or Marxism from this temporal-scope criticism; complete article and underlying books unread.

edges.relationship: Defends the regional and chronological scope of Slaves Without Masters against Ely’s reported charge that Berlin equates restrictive law with daily life.
edges.evidence_note: Own2004 Foner review permits generalizations, regional comparisons and change over1790–1860 that a single-county study cannot provide, while valuing Ely’s local research. This is an explicitly bounded reception intervention; it neither certifies all Berlin findings nor credits Berlin with writing Foner’s reply. Original books unread.

edges.relationship: Supplies Roediger with a formulation making African American family history central to the history of the working class.
edges.evidence_note: Selected indexed own1993 paragraph128 expressly quotes Berlin’s1987 Gutman introduction46. Berlin mediates Gutman’s research agenda; note2 co-credits Montgomery/Gutman/Rawick interviews and retains Brody’s range-of-positions qualification. Not a claim Berlin founded Roediger’s full argument; complete article and Berlin’s original introduction unread.

edges.relationship: Uses Curtin’s discussion of the expanding meanings of creole before specifying his own Atlantic-creole terminology.
edges.evidence_note: Own selected digital PartI note1 explicitly quotes and attributes Curtin Economic Change in Precolonial Africa1975 pp138–139n5, then warns that creole has no universally accepted usage and states his own definitions. This is bounded conceptual use from an authorial note, not a general genealogy or direct reading of Curtin’s complete book; cited original and continuous Berlin chapter unread.

edges.relationship: As Megan Hamilton reads the1999 response, Palmer contests Granatstein’s picture of a declining historical profession while also questioning the defensive self-satisfaction of its critics.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named mediation: Hamilton2021,28/notes44–45 identifies Palmer’s argument that historians are doing well and that defensive reaction to Granatstein has displaced critical reflection. The response is also directed at McKillop; Palmer is not flattened into McKillop’s camp. Original Palmer1999CHR80:4,676–686 and Granatstein’s1998book remain unread. Hamilton’s printed journal essay is a student scholarly publication, not treated as a direct reading of either original or as proof of every Palmer argument.

edges.relationship: Buckner contrasts Granatstein’s sweeping fragmentation charge with Owram’s more qualified pursuit of national synthesis that retains the value of recent social history.
edges.evidence_note: Own fresh reading of Buckner2000,9: he explicitly groups their fragmentation diagnoses but distinguishes Owram’s willingness to take the last30years of scholarship seriously and his acceptance of social history. Buckner himself contests both the hierarchy of national versus subdisciplinary history and the premise that regional history fragments Canada. An attributed comparison, not an Owram attack on Granatstein or an intellectual transmission. Granatstein1998 and Owram1997 original bodies unread.

edges.relationship: Greene qualifies Anderson’s account of intercolonial connections and challenges what he reads as an insufficiently lived and materially grounded account of corporate identity.
edges.evidence_note: Own2019answer explicitly accepts some mercantile links and the importance of Spanish imperial geography, but stresses competitive/local political identities and stronger transatlantic ties in other colonies. He then argues that corporate identities arise through economic practice, custom and legal culture. The suggestion that Anderson makes identity merely imaginary is Greene’s characterization, not certified here as a faithful account of Imagined Communities. Interviewer framing is distinct; Anderson1983original unread.

edges.relationship: Greene regards Bailyn’s emphasis on shared Atlantic processes as useful but favors comparison centered on differences and processes extending beyond the Atlantic basin.
edges.evidence_note: Own answer explicitly acknowledges the Atlantic’s internal dynamic and the utility of Bailyn’s short book, then recalls stressing differences on panels with him. This is a qualified methodological disagreement, not denial of all Atlantic connections, wholesale rejection of Bailyn or a claim to have originated comparative history. The interviewer’s paraphrase cites Neil Safier2010; Greene’s answer is distinct testimony. Bailyn’s book and Safier original unread.

edges.relationship: Greene credits cooperation with Mintz and Richard Price in sustaining the interdisciplinary Atlantic History and Culture program he helped organize at Johns Hopkins.
edges.evidence_note: Own retrospective answer identifies actual Anthropology Department cooperation over several decades and describes the original interdisciplinary program rather than mere shared employment. Richard Price retains joint credit; his endpoint is absent. This is a bounded collaborative intellectual setting, not proof of Mintz’s sole authorship, a specific book debt or personal formation. Precise institutional chronology not independently audited. Philip D.Morgan is a distinct absent-endpoint successor/coeditor, not Edmund S.Morgan.

edges.relationship: Greene qualifies Wood’s case for the Revolution’s radicalism by treating the later change in civic language as gradual, facilitated by independence and possibly achievable without it.
edges.evidence_note: Own2019answer grants the opening for new ways of talking about ordinary people and politics, then stresses a roughly fifty-year transition rather than an immediately radical event. His subsequent comparison emphasizes centralization in France and continuing composite authority in the United States. Friendship does not erase the disagreement. Wood’s complete books and R.R.Palmer’s1959work unread; Palmer is introduced by the interviewer. The reverse Wood→Greene critique and Greene→Wood contribution are already queued in Wood’s accepted packet, not duplicated here.

edges.relationship: Lears identifies Gramsci’s account of cultural hegemony as a framework for rethinking power, consent and cultural meaning in American history.
edges.evidence_note: Own1985explicitly adopts a framework and vocabulary while declining an uncritical embrace of the revolutionary program. Hoare/Nowell Smith’s1971Prison Notebooks translation and Lawner’s1973Letters are specified witnesses, not the complete Italian corpus. Own2010recollection retains Genovese and Davis as interpreters in his graduate intellectual environment.

edges.relationship: Lears questions Gramsci’s revolutionary teleology, rationalist psychology and rigid distinctions while retaining hegemony as a flexible historical method.
edges.evidence_note: Own critique singles out organic/traditional intellectuals, assumptions about workers’ authentic interests and a force/consent polarity. He concludes by affirming Gramsci’s openness to contradictory experience. This is not rejection of the entire method. Originals beyond the cited translated selections unread.

edges.relationship: Lears invokes Thompson’s unintended-consequences formulation and his account of law’s relative autonomy when explaining cultural meaning and power.
edges.evidence_note: Own Cohen answer expressly paraphrases Thompson, without establishing the original aphorism’s exact wording or source. Own1985p590uses Whigs and Hunters1975pp258–269 among plural models for ideology’s promise. Specific resources, not a claim to adopt all Thompson.

edges.relationship: Lears uses Williams’s account of feeling and cultural relations when developing a less mechanical conception of hegemony.
edges.evidence_note: Own1985invokes structure of feeling and identifies a parallel base/superstructure argument;1973article and The Long Revolution1961pp48–71 are distinct cited works. This is Raymond, not Eric Williams. Complete originals unread.

edges.relationship: Lears uses Genovese’s account of paternalism, accommodation and resistance to develop a historical analysis of hegemony.
edges.evidence_note: Own1985draws on Roll, Jordan, Roll1974pp585–665 and separately In Red and Black1970p369. He explicitly says his summary simplifies a complex argument; slaves’ dignity and resistance remain alongside accommodation. Whole books unread.

edges.relationship: Lears questions the classification of slave protest as prepolitical and the risk of making planter hegemony too static.
edges.evidence_note: Own578parenthesis places Genovese’s formulation beside Gramsci’s teleological limits;586reports criticism of a monolithic planter image while crediting Genovese’s sensitivity. It coexists with substantive use, not rejection of Roll, Jordan, Roll as a whole.

edges.relationship: Lears uses Hofstadter’s critique of the entrepreneurial consensus to frame how dissent can share dominant cultural commitments.
edges.evidence_note: Own576praises analytical insight but expressly denies making Hofstadter a Gramscian after the fact. The American Political Tradition1948 is cited atn19; the distinct Populism criticism concerns Age of Reform1955. Originals unread.

edges.relationship: Lears questions Hofstadter’s dismissal of Populism and failure to grasp efforts to build cultural alternatives.
edges.evidence_note: Own576contrasts Age of Reform’s agrarian-myth account with Lawrence Goodwyn’s reconstruction, retaining Goodwyn’s credit. His positive appraisal of Hofstadter’s entrepreneurial-consensus analysis remains separate.

edges.relationship: Lears uses Davis’s analysis of abolitionism’s unintended consequences to extend hegemony beyond deliberate social control.
edges.evidence_note: Own588/n50credits The Problem of Slavery in the Age of Revolution1974pp349–350, then extends the problem to private psychic needs. Robert Merton retains earlier general formulation credit. This is Lears’s use of a contested interpretation, not independent confirmation of Davis’s entire thesis. His2010mentor recollection is supplementary.

edges.relationship: Lears uses Foner’s account of artisans and price controls to show contradictions within producer ideology.
edges.evidence_note: Own575locates the shift from communal moral economy toward entrepreneurial expectations in Foner’s research. Plural surrounding reconstruction includes Laurie, Dawley, Hahn and Wilentz. Cited Tom Paine and Revolutionary America1976pp41,157 and chapter5; complete original unread.

edges.relationship: Lears invokes Woodward’s account of political coercion and fraud as necessary context for explaining Populism’s defeat.
edges.evidence_note: Own576credits Origins of the New South1877–1913(1951) while extending the analysis through Goodwyn’s cultural account. Political coercion is not replaced by an exclusively symbolic explanation. Complete original unread.

edges.relationship: Lears uses Weber’s treatment of hypothetical nonoccurrences to frame inquiry into unrealized historical possibilities.
edges.evidence_note: Own585/n44specifies Critical Studies in the Logic of the Cultural Sciences in Shils/Finch1949Methodology of the Social Sciences,164–188. This methodological resource is distinct from loose Weberian-modernity language in the Serlin interview. LaCapra/Heidegger retain separate credit for thinking the unthought. Complete cited original unread.

edges.relationship: Lears draws on Bourdieu’s work on education and taste as a model for investigating cultural reproduction.
edges.evidence_note: Own589credits Bourdieu while insisting that actual audience/student experience remains to be studied. Reproduction is jointly authored with J.C.Passeron(cited1977edition); Distinction is cited in Richard Nice’s1984translation. These are plural methodological resources, not verified complete readings here.

edges.relationship: Lears questions how Geertzian cultural analysis can obscure unequal power and larger political-economic structures.
edges.evidence_note: Own573criticizes both an implicit functionalism and historians’ uses of symbolic systems. Own586–587credits Rhys Isaac with overcoming that limitation rather than treating all Geertz-inspired history as defective. Original Geertz1973collection unread.

edges.relationship: Lears questions antisubjectivist readings of Foucault and their capacity to explain agency and a shared political good.
edges.evidence_note: Own1985recognizes salutary effects of socially constituted subjectivity before objecting to mechanistic agency-denial. Own2010distinguishes Foucault’s useful surveillance analysis from an individualist academic reception; it is not a claim that every recipient interpretation is Foucault’s own doctrine. Cited original books unread.

edges.relationship: Lears uses White’s account of semiotic codes to ask how discourse establishes plausibility beyond fixed ideological binaries.
edges.evidence_note: Own590adopts the question while reserving criticism of White’s subsequent Adams reading. Cited1982essay Method and Ideology in Intellectual History, in LaCapra/Kaplan edited Modern European Intellectual History,288–289; original essay unread.

edges.relationship: Lears questions White’s emphasis on nihilism in Henry Adams, arguing that it overlooks vitalism, religious longing and Marian Adams.
edges.evidence_note: Own593/n62singles out a particular reading, credits its skill and distinguishes it from the useful semiotic questions adopted earlier. White’s1982essay290–310 and Adams’s full Education unread here; no verdict on all White’s narrative theory.

edges.relationship: Lears uses Lefebvre’s concern about depleted signs in consumer culture to question celebratory accounts of struggles over meaning.
edges.evidence_note: Own592gives plural credit to Lefebvre, Baudrillard and William Leiss, with Stephen Kline jointly credited in one cited study. Lefebvre source is Everyday Life in the Modern World, Sacha Rabinovitch translation1971p119. No entire translated book read.

edges.relationship: Lears questions the historical usefulness of Habermas’s ideal speech situation as a possible alternative to hegemonic discourse.
edges.evidence_note: Own585regards completely undistorted communication as too remote for this historical task, then proposes inquiry into nearer unrealized possibilities. Cites What Is Universal Pragmatics? in Communication and the Evolution of Society, Thomas McCarthy translation1979p63. This is a task-specific limitation, not rejection of all Habermas; original unread.

edges.relationship: Lears finds Pocock’s linguistic history helpful but too intellectualist for the cultural-hegemony inquiry he outlines.
edges.evidence_note: Own qualified note concerns Politics, Language, and Time1971,3–41; it accompanies proposals to study broader cultural texts and symbolic practices. No blanket rejection of intellectual history or a claim to have read Pocock’s entire book.

edges.relationship: Lears uses Hall and the Birmingham Centre’s reciprocal model of cultural meaning before qualifying its account of subcultural resistance.
edges.evidence_note: Own590names Hall and colleagues;591n56cites both a Centre collection and Resistance through Rituals, jointly edited by Hall and Tony Jefferson(cited1975). Hall is not sole author of every case study. The example supplies a point of departure, not uncritical endorsement; originals unread.

edges.relationship: Lears questions whether Hall and Birmingham’s bricolage framework sufficiently explains the character of youth resistance.
edges.evidence_note: Own590–591moves from the named Hall/collective account of Teddy Boys to the objection that celebration alone is insufficient, then proposes Bakhtin’s multivalence. Collective authors and coeditor Tony Jefferson retain credit; no claim that all Hall writing celebrates consumption.

edges.relationship: McKay adopts and extends Lears’s definition of antimodernism when explaining the construction of Scottish Nova Scotia.
edges.evidence_note: Own McKay1992p9/n12quotes No Place of Grace1981p xv and adds simple life and nature. Personal resource is demonstrated by this use, not co-citation. Existing edge895is a McKay→Canadian field contribution; no duplicate field edge or inference that all Quest of the Folk1994was read. Lears’s original book remains unread.

edges.relationship: Wickberg reads Lears as combining Freudian unconscious motivation with Gramscian cultural legitimation in No Place of Grace.
edges.evidence_note: Named2016scholarly mediation identifies a specific conceptual combination and criticizes its sometimes mechanical implementation. This does not verify direct reading of a particular Freud edition or turn the whole book into an unqualified psychoanalytic scheme. Gramsci retains distinct credit; Lears1981and Freud originals unread.

edges.relationship: Lears uses deconstructionist attention to intertextuality and multiple meanings as a resource for moving beyond binary cultural interpretations.
edges.evidence_note: Own591gives joint conceptual credit to Derrida and Paul de Man, alongside a distinct Bakhtin argument. Cites Derrida, Dissemination, Barbara Johnson translation1981; the later criticism of antisubjectivism remains separate. Original untranslated/translated book unread.

edges.relationship: Lears questions the denial of the human subject in Derridean polemics while retaining insights into constructed selfhood.
edges.evidence_note: Own592identifies Derrida’s metaphysics-of-presence critique and593objects to losing agency and historical change. This is a qualified criticism of the tendency discussed, not a claim that every Derrida text is mechanistic. Cited1983Alan Bass translation Margins of Philosophy unread.

edges.relationship: Lears questions Althusser’s account of subjective will as ideological illusion within his broader criticism of antisubjectivism.
edges.evidence_note: Own592singles out Althusser, then593argues that historians need subjectivity to explain resistance and transformation. Cited Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses in Lenin and Philosophy and Other Essays, Ben Brewster translation1971,127–186. No complete original reading or general refutation of all structural Marxism.

edges.relationship: Lears takes up Lévi-Strauss’s bricolage concept through Hall and Birmingham’s account of youth culture, then questions its explanatory limits.
edges.evidence_note: Own590–591expressly identifies Lévi-Strauss as the concept’s source and Hall/colleagues as intermediaries. The concept is a point of departure in Lears’s discussion, not a claim to have read a specified Lévi-Strauss original or to endorse a wholly celebratory account. Hall, Tony Jefferson and the Centre retain separate credit.

edges.relationship: McPherson credits Woodward’s example of combining new historical interpretation with prose for a broad audience as shaping his approach to writing.
edges.evidence_note: His own NEH answer specifies Tom Watson, Origins of the New South and Strange Career of Jim Crow and Woodward’s criticism of his writing. Lindley answer explicitly identifies a formative influence on writing. Distinct kind from existing edge_1799 commissioning contribution; no claim that every interpretation derives from Woodward, or new reading of the named books or draft materials.

edges.relationship: McPherson names Hofstadter as a formative model for historical writing that reaches academic and interested lay audiences.
edges.evidence_note: Own recollection explicitly joins Hofstadter with Allan Nevins and Arthur Schlesinger Jr.; all retain credit. This is a writing/audience influence during graduate school and after, not evidence that McPherson adopted consensus historiography or a specified Hofstadter book. No original reading of those authors in this dossier.

edges.relationship: McPherson uses Foner’s account of fugitive slaves and interracial aid networks to explain how a numerically small movement intensified sectional conflict.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2015 review endorses the political force of escapees and publicizes Foner’s New York evidence. Madeline Lewis’s discovery of Gay’s Record of Fugitives, Gay and Louis Napoleon’s work and enslaved people’s initiative retain credit. Specific resource in this essay, not a claim that Foner originated McPherson’s broader emancipation interpretation. Full Gateway to Freedom and record independently unread.

edges.relationship: McPherson draws on Faust’s account of the Good Death and the wartime/postwar identification and reburial of soldiers to connect mourning with new national obligations.
edges.evidence_note: Specific argumentative use in own 2008 review coexists with his reservations about theology and weighting costs against achievements. Mark Schantz supplies a distinct complementary account of the culture of death; Faust is not credited with his claims. Original This Republic of Suffering unread. The reverse-direction criticism key is already reserved by Faust’s queued dossier and is not duplicated.

edges.relationship: Credits Société féodale with showing that collective sentiments and daily activities are significant historical objects.
edges.evidence_note: Own2010 retrospective441 says the influence of Bloch’s book remained woven through his writing after reading it at the École normale supérieure. Named conceptual debt, not merely institutional affiliation; complete Bloch original unread. Preserves1939–1940 title as cited without implying an English translation appeared then.

edges.relationship: Credits Ariès’s study of childhood and family life as an important model of historical inquiry.
edges.evidence_note: Own2010 retrospective441 names L’enfant et la vie de famille dans la France d’Ancien Régime and calls it a masterpiece while acknowledging criticism of it. Admiration is not converted into agreement with every thesis or a formal teaching relation. Complete original book and criticisms unread.

edges.relationship: Credits Febvre’s questions with directing his histories of fear, security and first communion.
edges.evidence_note: Own signed Lettre6 p27 attributes initial fear inquiry to a1956 article; own2010 p440 answers a1952 book-review question about security and p446 recalls a suggestion to historicize first communion. These are separate prompts, not one reconstructed text or a claim of exclusive invention. Own2010 p441 additionally values Luther study. Underlying Febvre sources unread.

edges.relationship: Guides Delumeau’s archival research on Rome and alum and provides a model of broad context and longue durée.
edges.evidence_note: Own2010 pp436–437 credits Gaston Zeller’s thesis-topic advice and Braudel’s research guidance; Braudel is called primary adviser but contemporaneous formal degree-supervision restrictions are explicitly explained. Do not equate intellectual guidance with an inspected formal supervisor record.441–442 names Mediterranean as methodological example despite Braudel’s different interests; original books unread.

edges.relationship: Invokes Duby as a model of writing for a broad public and an ally in interpreting the Reformations as a renewal of Christianization.
edges.evidence_note: Own2010 p442 includes Duby among historians whose writing/research offered an example; p444 explicitly attributes the renewal interpretation to him. No particular Duby title is identified here, and underlying texts were not inspected. This is Delumeau’s stated appropriation, not formal mentorship or a claim that every medievalist shares his thesis.

edges.relationship: Uses The Cult of Saints in discussing the persistence and transformation of religious practices under Christian forms.
edges.evidence_note: Own2010 p444/n22 characterizes Brown as illustrating functions transferred from pagan gods to saints. This is Delumeau’s reading, not certification that Brown endorses Delumeau’s entire pagan-veneer thesis. Original Brown book unread; note22’s1980 bibliographic year is not separately certified or used to alter canonical chronology.

edges.relationship: Adopts Le Goff’s description of Christendom around1500 as still nearly mission territory in arguing for late intensive Christianization.
edges.evidence_note: Own1975 p58 says he thinks with LeGoff and cites Le christianisme médiéval, Histoire des religionsII,1972,p856 in note8. Underlying chapter unread; this does not make medieval Europe uniformly pagan or erase Delumeau’s later2010 p444 qualification of provocative wording. No inference from shared schooling or Annales membership.

edges.relationship: Uses Vovelle’s testamentary research as the starting point for a methodological reflection on dechristianization.
edges.evidence_note: Own1975 pp52–56 praises Piété baroque et déchristianisation1973 as a pioneering, rigorous and nuanced inquiry, then examines conclusions drawn from it. At58 he calls quantitative inquiry legitimate and indispensable for the institutional Christianity it measures. Original Vovelle book unread; praise is distinct from total methodological equivalence.

edges.relationship: Distinguishes Vovelle’s quantitative history of religious practice from a qualitative history of different Christian models.
edges.evidence_note: Own1975 pp56–60 explicitly calls this a methodological dialogue, says the chosen dossier is unassailable within its horizons and warns hasty readers against extrapolating religion’s complete disappearance. The comparison is undirected and not a claim Vovelle himself predicted Christianity’s death. Both approaches have distinct objects and can coexist; no manufactured personal quarrel.

edges.relationship: As reported by Paillard, cautions that Freud’s negative critique of religion crosses disciplinary methods and documentary limits.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh introductory17 is Bernard Paillard’s account of Delumeau’s interdisciplinary position, not a verbatim Delumeau answer.18–23 do not supply an additional direct Freud criticism. The named reported objection remains particular; no Freud title or universal rejection of psychology/psychoanalysis is invented, and original Freud works unread.

edges.relationship: As Jorge M.Escobar explains, O’Brien uses Latour’s purification and translation concepts to analyze settlers’ claims to exclusive modernity and Indigenous disappearance.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation in Escobar’s actual indexed chapter116and127/n6, corroborated by O’Brien’s own selected indexedxxi–xxii/3–4 passages. Escobar distinguishes purification/translation and applies the framework to New Granada; his extension is not attributed to O’Brien. Full O’Brien chapter/pages and Latour original unread. Escobarn3distinguishes1991French original; O’Brien’s indexed214reference names Catherine Porter’s translation but renders a1991date, not collated against an image or silently certified as an English edition date.

edges.relationship: O’Brien uses Trouillot’s account of unequal historical production and archival power to analyze local histories and public commemoration.
edges.evidence_note: Own selected public indexedxvii/xxiand56explicitly name Trouillot when widening historical production beyond professional historians, treating local histories as an archive, and considering public meanings made through commemoration. A particular theoretical resource, not sole genealogy or a claim that the full primary pages were read. Selected214indexednote names Silencing the Past,55; complete endnotes/edition and Trouillot original unread.

edges.relationship: O’Brien credits Calloway’s helpful reading of the entire Firsting and Lasting manuscript.
edges.evidence_note: Own public indexed acknowledgment207explicitly identifies his manuscript reading. The same selected context credits Jim Merrell’s reading of nearly every chapter and repeated introduction advice, and a Jennifer whose surname is not visible in the selected extract. Those distinct contributions are not assigned to Calloway. Bounded manuscript assistance, not proof of doctrinal agreement, coauthorship or an independently verified complete-book reading.

edges.relationship: Wolfe uses O’Brien’s evidence on New England treaty status and earlier blood-quantum practices in his history of Indigenous racialization and dispossession.
edges.evidence_note: Own fresh selected2016body and actual endnotes: chapter5/n30uses Firsting203for disadvantages facing tribes dispossessed before US treaty relationships; chapter6/n92uses Firsting128for an earlier Connecticut blood-quantum example. These are two specific resources within one pair/kind, not evidence that O’Brien endorsed Wolfe’s entire comparative framework. O’Brien’s cited pages remain unread in full; Wolfe’s original legal/historical sources are not independently checked. Ebook PDF pagination is explicit and not passed off as print pages.

edges.relationship: Black challenges the modernisation-as-secularisation premise he attributes jointly to Durkheim and Weber, arguing that its secular concept of reason obscures past military cultures.
edges.evidence_note: Own2020 chapter27 explicitly names both sociologists before criticizing the premise’s circularity, selective evidence and failure to understand past military values. This is Black’s bounded collective attribution and critique; his preceding26distinction between Durkheimian constraints and Weberian contingent outcomes is retained. Neither sociologist’s original texts were collated; no claim that their complete theories are identical, that either personally influenced Black, or that every military-revolution proponent follows them.

edges.relationship: Colley praised Black’s documentation but sought an explanation of tourism’s effects on British self-understanding.
edges.evidence_note: Own review; final two paragraphs. Book unread. Praise and reservation coexist.

edges.relationship: Responding to Janowski’s Marx/Mill comparison, Black rejects deterministic historical teleology as empirically and morally flawed because it effaces complexity, free will and moral choice.
edges.evidence_note: Own final2020interview answer138addresses Janowski’s explicitly repeated Marx/Mill interpretation, following the quoted comparison134–135. This is an interviewer-framed critique of a particular attributed vision, not an independent collation of Marx’s writings or a claim that every Marxian account is identical. The interviewer’s quotation is attributed to Marx without edition/coauthor detail; Marx/Engels originals were not collated and sole authorship is not asserted. Mill co-subject retained, exact endpoint absent. Black’s broader political claims remain his2020testimony, not certified current facts.

edges.relationship: Brewer recalls Bailyn’s treatment of political ideology and his methodological criticism as shaping Brewer’s approach to eighteenth-century popular politics.
edges.evidence_note: Own2026 names Ideological Origins and its press/dissemination argument; later Harvard recollection explicitly calls his work inspired by Bailyn and credits questioning that widened an overly narrow party-politics focus. Skinner and Davis/Turner retain distinct credit. Patronage alone is not the basis; no original book/draft reading.

edges.relationship: Brewer credits Skinner’s contextual treatment of political arguments as actions with helping him take political ideas seriously in his social history of politics.
edges.evidence_note: Own2026 explains lectures’ appeal and later explicitly names lessons learned from Skinner and Bailyn in his alternative to Namier. Wittgenstein/Austin are Skinner’s philosophical resources, not demonstrated direct Brewer reading. No claim all later work follows a Cambridge School doctrine.

edges.relationship: Brewer recalls Davis’s Rites of Violence lecture turning him toward anthropological analysis of political ritual and symbol.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit 2026 account connects lecture to his interpretation of eighteenth-century protests and names Victor Turner’s Ritual Process as a subsequent distinct resource, with Van Gennep upstream. No direct original lecture text or Turner book read, no retrospective lecture date invented. His2010 use of Davis is additional later methodological witness.

edges.relationship: Brewer identifies Weber’s analysis of bureaucracy as a comparative resource for The Sinews of Power.
edges.evidence_note: Own2026 retains Skocpol’s mediation, Hintze’s parallel war/state-formation contribution, Mathias/O’Brien’s joint taxation argument and the CES institutionalist circle. He used the excise as an exemplary bureaucracy but denies making it a general model of English administration. No specified Weber edition, complete original book or unconditional agreement claimed.

edges.relationship: Brewer identifies Thompson and the Warwick law/history debate as a starting point refined in An Ungovernable People and his inquiry into governance.
edges.evidence_note: Own2026 calls the1980 volume an explicit engagement developing/refining views of law’s role in social relations. John Styles coeditor and other contributors retain credit. Distinct from the unspecified Making disagreements recalled in teaching; no claim Thompson supplied every conclusion or that the original1980 volume was read.

edges.relationship: Brewer credits Habermas’s public-sphere analysis with later clarifying the popular-politics inquiry he had developed independently.
edges.evidence_note: Own2026 expressly says he did not know Habermas when writing Party Ideology(1976);1962 German original and1989 English translation are distinguished. Later UCLA deliberations used public sphere alongside diverse approaches. No influence backdated to1976 or original Habermas reading in this dossier.

edges.relationship: Brewer names Foucault’s analysis of authorship and relations between knowledge and power among the resources used in the Cultures of Consumption project.
edges.evidence_note: Own retrospective identifies a specific concept within collective deliberations led by Brewer, Porter, Staves and Bermingham. Diverse participants differed and some ignored theory; no uniform adoption or formative influence by every contributor. Porter’s criticism of Foucault and feminist theories retain separate credit. Original works/editions not specified or read.

edges.relationship: Brewer names Bourdieu’s analysis of taste and distinction among the resources used in the Cultures of Consumption project.
edges.evidence_note: Own retrospective identifies a specific concept within collective deliberations led by Brewer, Porter, Staves and Bermingham. Diverse participants differed and some ignored theory; no uniform adoption or formative influence by every contributor. Porter’s criticism of Foucault and feminist theories retain separate credit. Original works/editions not specified or read.

edges.relationship: Brewer and Porter shared an interdisciplinary consumption project that brought varied historical approaches together in Consumption and the World of Goods.
edges.evidence_note: Undirected shared editorial/research project, not mutual influence or shared authorship of all essays. Own2026 names Porter as first Clark professor and workshops/lectures format;1993 catalogue identifies both editors and individual chapter authors. Staves and Bermingham led subsequent distinct years/volumes. Disagreement and individual voice retained.

edges.relationship: Brewer uses Ginzburg’s account of clues, constructed research and incomplete historical truth to explain microhistory’s humanist realism.
edges.evidence_note: Own2010 uses cited1989 Clues96–125,1993 Microhistory23–24/27/32–33 and Wooden Eyes2001p156; John/Anne C.Tedeschi translation credit retained for Clues and the1993 English essay; Wooden Eyes is translated by Martin Ryle and Kate Soper. Kracauer and Pallares-Burke remain explicit intermediaries where cited. Constructed interpretation is not equated with fiction or completeness; original works unread.

edges.relationship: Brewer uses Levi’s account of scale and negotiated agency to explain what microhistorical inquiry can reveal.
edges.evidence_note: Own2010 distinguishes methodological shifts of observation from narrative completeness. Cited On Microhistory in Peter Burke ed.(1991)94–98/106/110 and Origins of the Modern State(1998)58–62 are reader locators, not fresh originals. The same essay’s specific reservation is separately retained.

edges.relationship: Brewer questions claims that microhistorical scale yields total history and finds Levi’s state-origins argument insufficiently dependent on microhistorical methods.
edges.evidence_note: Own2010 n58 calls the specific1998 attempt largely unsuccessful; printed97 criticism addresses an aspiration among some French/Italian microhistorians, not all Levi writing. He accepts shifts of scale as plausible and useful and uses Levi positively elsewhere. No complete original essay read.

edges.relationship: Brewer uses Chartier’s account of reduced-scale inquiry to connect beliefs and representations with social affiliations without deterministic reduction.
edges.evidence_note: Own2010 printed97 explicitly introduces Chartier as explaining dynamic interconnections. N53 cites chapterp32 as1981; institutional catalogues date the LaCapra/Kaplan edited volume1982, discrepancy retained. Additional n71 On Edge of Cliff citation not confused with appointment support. Complete original chapter/translated book unread.

edges.relationship: Brewer uses de Certeau’s contrast between the view from above and street-level experience to clarify the powers and limits of historical perspective.
edges.evidence_note: Own2010 makes the World Trade Center passage a metaphor for prospect/refuge histories. Note61 identifies The Practice of Everyday Life(1984),92, Steven Rendall translation; body loosely calls it History of Everyday Life. Separate Writing of History/Heterologies citations not collapsed into that book. Original French/English full books unread.

edges.relationship: Brewer draws on Lefebvre’s critique of managed consumption and his reading of everyday life through Ulysses when explaining the politics of small-scale history.
edges.evidence_note: Own2010 identifies a humanist critical tradition with de Certeau and others, contrasts consumerist modernization, and uses literary access to daily experience. Brewer cites New York1984 edition chapter2 and3–7; Sacha Rabinovitch English translation distinguished from original French and later reissues. Complete work unread.

edges.relationship: Brewer uses Cohen’s account of American commodities as symbols of a liberal democratic way of life in his explanation of Cold War consumption.
edges.evidence_note: Own2010 explicitly credits Cohen alongside de Grazia’s earlier genealogy and other scholarly resources. Cited A Consumers’ Republic(2003) and Citizens and Consumers essay in Daunton/Hilton eds.(2001); neither original read. Specific resource in this historiographical argument, not broad formative influence.

edges.relationship: Brewer invokes Scott’s critique of experiential immediacy to frame a limit of histories claiming direct access to lived experience.
edges.evidence_note: Own2010 identifies the criticism in Evidence of Experience(1991) and distinguishes Althusser’s earlier account from historical-source critiques by Finlay/Kuehn. This is a resource framing a problem, not endorsement of every claim or a direct critique by Brewer of Davis’s entire work. Scott’s original essay unread.

edges.relationship: Stone praises The Sinews of Power while questioning its chronology, cultural explanation, claims of administrative probity and fiscal-military label.
edges.evidence_note: Own1990 final section asks for1793–1815, more attention to attitudes and opposition, and questions efficient honest offices. He proposes warfare-welfare state to include poor relief while strongly crediting Brewer’s revision. These are Stone’s arguments; no independent statistical replication or complete book reading.

edges.relationship: Stone uses Brewer’s account of taxation, borrowing and parliamentary authority to explain Britain’s war-making capacity and compare it with French fiscal weakness.
edges.evidence_note: Own1990 explicitly calls Brewer’s finance analysis convincing and draws it into a comparative argument before offering objections. Not an origin claim: Stone says earlier scholars established details and adds his own welfare qualification. Full Brewer book unread; concrete resource in Stone’s review.

edges.relationship: As reported by Ruiz, Ginzburg credits Brewer’s suggestion of a connection between Italian microhistory and neorealist cinema as plausible for his own experience.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named mediation: Ruiz2008note1 reproduces Ginzburg’s2007 Hindu interview answer to Subrahmanyam. Tentative recognition of a specific suggestion, not Brewer’s formative influence on Ginzburg or verified causal derivation of all microhistory. Original interview unread; Zavattini and Ginzburg’s earlier film interests retain credit.

edges.relationship: Brewer recalls siding with Ginzburg in the1990 representation debate and finding the skeptic’s standard of historical truth excessively demanding.
edges.evidence_note: Own2026 explicitly frames the Ginzburg–White encounter, recognizes that Ginzburg accepted constructed writing and White analyzed rhetoric, and rejects a crude positivist/relativist binary. Criticism concerns the expectations in this dispute and favors qualified knowledge; no claim White denied the Holocaust or fresh original conference-paper reading.

edges.relationship: Brewer uses Ariès’s account of criticism of progress moving from the Right toward the Left to explain interest in preindustrial societies and mentalities.
edges.evidence_note: Own2010 printed93 attributes the claim to Ariès, mediated in n27 by Ginzburg’s1993 Microhistory p20. It contributes to Brewer’s explanation of intellectual disillusionment alongside Gregory and Revel. No direct Ariès work/title or original reading established; the mediated route is explicit, not a formative influence claim.

edges.relationship: Brewer uses Cannadine’s account of British industrialization as a model for later economic-development policy in his analysis of Cold War modernization.
edges.evidence_note: Own2010 printed94/n33 cites Cannadine’s The Present and the Past in the English Industrial Revolution,1880–1980, Past and Present103(1984),147–148and152–154, for the discussion including the policy formulation. Brewer separately cites Rostow1971p33 in n35. Cannadine is a scholarly resource for the historical relationship, not credited with endorsing Rostow’s political program; neither original work read.

edges.relationship: Uses Bloch to explain the historian’s indirect access to the past and the limits of immediate eyewitness experience.
edges.evidence_note: Own selected first-chapter argument invokes the tiny patch of events available to an individual, and chapter3’s publisher-displayed opening uses Bloch’s reconstruction/residue analogy. First-chapter note6 names Peter Putnam’s English translation, Manchester1992 reprint of1953 translation. Neither Bloch original nor complete Gaddis book inspected; no literal time-travel or experimental-replication claim.

edges.relationship: Refers to Benjamin’s Illuminations as a comparable artistic metaphor for the historian’s backward-looking perspective.
edges.evidence_note: Specific own first-chapter note4, attached to the historian’s back-turned posture, identifies Illuminations, Harry Zohn translation, NewYork1968,p257. A bounded conceptual comparison used by Gaddis, not formal mentorship or direct inspection of Benjamin’s German text. The source’s particular reverse-facing image is not generalized to agreement with Benjamin’s philosophy of history.

edges.relationship: Cites Telling the Truth about History in acknowledging the situated character of historical judgment.
edges.evidence_note: Own first-chapter passage beginning We have, in recent years, embraced postmodernist insights, and note17, co-credit Joyce Appleby and Margaret Jacob as authors of the1994book and also cite Evans/Ferguson/Bloch/Carr. Note24 additionally references the jointly authored book for observer/reconstruction problems. No soleHuntauthorship, no general pupil genealogy, no claim that all these scholars share one theory; original jointbook unread.

edges.relationship: Uses Ferguson’s Virtual History essay as a reference for the situated character of historical judgments.
edges.evidence_note: Own first-chapter note17 and attached observer/judgment paragraph, with Evans, Appleby/Hunt/Jacob, Bloch and Carr co-credited. This is a specific cited methodological resource, not a claim Gaddis endorses every counterfactual or Ferguson’s imperial arguments. Original Ferguson essay and remainder of the edited collection unread; edition year not inferred from shortened Gaddis note.

edges.relationship: Criticizes The Cold War: A New History for a US-centered triumphalist narrative that marginalizes other societies, culture and continuing legacies.
edges.evidence_note: Own signed2006review sections1–3 targets a particular popular book: Soviet perspectives, ThirdWorld costs, differences among WesternEuropeans and cultural/generational conflict, plus connections after1989. Judt acknowledges Gaddis’s earlier archival achievements and treats We Now Know as a different work. No claim that Judt discovered every alleged factual error correctly or that this exhausts Gaddis’s scholarship; complete reviewed book unread.

edges.relationship: Credits Foner as her adviser and a central model for historical scholarship, teaching and public engagement.
edges.evidence_note: Her own acknowledgment on p. xv calls Foner her adviser and her biggest debt, while also naming other Columbia teachers. Her 1999 article, p. 67, acknowledges support and constructive criticism. No single proprietary theory, sole authorship or independently inspected degree file is inferred. The acknowledgment was read in the 2014 reprint; the 2004 printing was not collated.

edges.relationship: Uses Jacobson’s account of whiteness and credits his reading of the Impossible Subjects manuscript.
edges.evidence_note: The 1999 article, p. 70 and note 9, explicitly attributes the formulation of a consanguine white race to Matthew Jacobson and identifies Whiteness of a Different Color (1998). The work identifies Matthew Frye Jacobson rather than a namesake. The reprinted acknowledgment, p. xvi, names him among readers of all or part of the penultimate draft. The conceptual and manuscript roles are consolidated here; his original book remains unread.

edges.relationship: Credits Gerstle’s intellectual and editorial interventions with improving Impossible Subjects.
edges.evidence_note: The acknowledgment, p. xvii, singles out Gerstle while also crediting series editors William Chafe, Linda Gordon and Julian Zelizer. The 1999 author note acknowledges his support and constructive criticism; the 2014 foreword, note 4, lists American Crucible among resources on racial history. Other editors' contributions are not assigned to him, and editorial assistance is not formal supervision. His original books remain unread.

edges.relationship: Uses Anderson’s imagined-community framework to historicize the nation and question nationalist assumptions in immigration history.
edges.evidence_note: The introduction, p. 9, and the new 2014 foreword, p. xxi, explicitly invoke Anderson. The 1999 article, note 8, also cites Imagined Communities alongside Hobsbawm, Balakrishnan and Gilroy. This is a specific conceptual use, not agreement with all nationalism theory. Anderson's original book remains unread, and its editions are not conflated.

edges.relationship: Uses Gilroy’s insistence on historically specific racisms in analyzing legal racial categories.
edges.evidence_note: The introduction, p. 7, directly attributes the historical specificity of racism to Gilroy before developing the argument about classification in the 1920s. The 1999 article, note 8, also lists The Black Atlantic, but the preview lacks the original introduction's note 14, so the exact source of the quoted formula is not invented.
